Back to life in the rhythm of the waters
The global crises of biodiversity and cultural diversity are interdependent, especially
so in rivers. While we know that 84% of the freshwater fauna has disappeared between
1970 and 2014, the loss in cultural diversity connect­ed to the river and its floodplain
(e.g., spiritual linkages, traditional use forms, adapted architecture, etc.) is as yet un-
known.

This book makes a first attempt to deal with biological and
cultural diversities altogether, depicting the bio-cul-
tural diversities, historical human-river relation-
ships, threats, and practical examples of how to
mitigate the crisis in riverscapes. More than
120 authors present interdisciplinary studies
from river systems all over the world, and

and governments are invited to disseminate the
positive examples presented here, to document their
own work, and to contribute to a more harmonious and
peaceful life in riverscapes.

Foreword


Inland waters only represent 0.001% of the water that makes our planet a blue one, and rivers are
only a fraction of this, but still, they represent most of the water that we all, humans and other spe-
cies on earth, need to maintain their lives. Rivers are an analogy to life, and it is not surprising that
all over the world, they have been and are worshipped as symbols for permanent change, for purity,
for fertility and their support to all kinds of life and culture. Rivers feature multiple economic and
natural aspects of civilization and therefore reflect changing human values over time. In a physical
context, they convey water and sediments from land to sea and change the surface of the earth. Life
sciences identify the adaptations of diverse animal and plant species to a permanently changing en-
vironment and the great importance of rivers to connect distant habitats for migratory species. Hu-
man culture has taken up these functions, as rivers and valleys have been the cradle of humankind,
of the first settlements and agriculture in the floodplains, but also the corridors in which human cul-
ture has been communicated and the human species has been dispersed. In the Anthropocene, these
life-support functions and the bio-cultural diversity of riverscapes often reflect human-environment
conflicts. The social processes that drive such conflicts leading to degradation are very similar, de-
spite strongly varying cultural backgrounds in different parts of the world.
   The present book "River Culture – Life as a Dance to the Rhythm of the Waters" is contributing to
UNESCO's efforts to harmonize humans with nature and to avoid human conflicts. By applying an
interdisciplinary approach, it brings together the social and ecological background information on
28 selected river basins all over the world, shows the connectedness of people to their rivers, but also
the menaces, and finally, practical approaches and suggestions to mitigate these problems. It thereby
contributes to UNESCO's Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme (IHP) and the Sustainable
Development Goals (SDGs) by the United Nations, mostly on SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation),
and indirectly to all other SDGs. As a source of exchange, innovation and creativity, cultural diver-
sity is as necessary for humankind as biodiversity is for nature. The UNESCO Universal Declaration
on Cultural Diversity (2001) has become an additional pillar to the co-construction of sustainability
targets and approaches, and the intercultural comparison provided by this book contributes to a
better understanding of the previously unassessed cultural diversity connected with rivers.
   Special attention is given to the equality of contributions from the Global North and the Global
South, documented by the large proportion of case studies from the Global South. Another focus is
on the equality of women and men, which is of the current key priorities of UNESCO. In traditional
societies, rivers have contributed to structuring gender roles. The cultural decline is eroding these
structures, often to the detriment of women. A specific chapter has been dedicated to delivering a
baseline for future studies on this issue. Further chapters go beyond the general catchment-based
structure of the chapters and are dealing with urgent overarching issues such as urbanization, river
fragmentation by dams, governance issues and the ecosocial concept of sustainable development.
Special contributions have been made by artists through the process, who provided a universal lan-
guage of art for symbolizing the interactions between humans and nature.

      Prof. Shahbaz Khan, Director and UNESCO Representative to the People's Republic of China,
             the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Japan, Mongolia and the Republic of Korea
                                                                                                     VII


Preface


Like a river, this book coalesced from different sources. During the formation of the River Culture
concept and the first workshops organized by the UNESCO Chair in 2014, ideas for a book that
synthesizes historical and present-day knowledge on both, the biological and cultural adaptations
in floodplains, were drafted. The book gained momentum from the initiative by the late Professor
Brij Gopal (see dedication below) to produce a multi-authored book. The strongest support for this
book (and its mainstem, to stay with the river analogy) was the "2nd Great Rivers Forum", orga-
nized by the UNESCO Beijing Office and the Changjiang Civilization Museum in Wuhan, China,
on October 28–30, 2018. Thanks to the generous support of the Wuhan Municipal Government, this
meeting enabled a gathering of river knowledge holders, including scientists, managers, and practi-
tioners from all over the world. Expert sessions included: (i) River Culture: Preserve and Let Evolve
Natural and Cultural Heritages of Great Rivers, (ii) Visualizing Water Worlds along Great Riv-
ers – Water Museums, Heritage, Memory and Sense of Place, (iii) Urban Development along Great
Rivers – Reconnecting the City with Its River, (iv) Water-related UNESCO Designated Sites (WH
sites, Biosphere Reserves, Creative Cities) and (v) a High-level Roundtable on The Integration of
River Culture and Environment in the Management of Great River Basins. This open dialogue and
exchange of ideas was held online and has received 16,797 million reads and 7,989 discussion con-
tributions in China, in addition to countless inputs from other participants elsewhere in the world.
   These beginnings served to bring together, through this book project, social and natural scientists
engaged in the protection and maintenance of the bio-cultural diversities of river floodplains by em-
ploying a truly interdisciplinary approach. Authors from all over the world were invited to identify
ideas that could be useful for this purpose, by observing adaptive strategies in nature and cultural
use forms, based on traditional ecological knowledge that could be directly applied or transformed
for current-day management practices. They also aimed to communicate innovative approaches re-
sulting from the interdisciplinary exchanges and to document successful initiatives for the bio-cul-
tural management of rivers that could serve as examples for other places.
   Many people have contributed to this book, in total, 125 authors from 24 countries (fig. 1). The 36
chapters include 28 case studies of rivers from 4 continents (Africa: 6, Asia: 7, Americas: 6, Europe: 9,
fig. 2). They all follow the same structure, enabeling direct comparisons to be made among the di-
verse river systems covered. The chapters compare the geophysical and historical setting, and bio-
logical and cultural diversities, and then go further to describe trends influencing these diversities
and management options that may help to mitigate socio-ecological problems. Identical tables sup-
port comparisons between the diverse river systems. The remainder 8 chapters synthesize aspects of
artists' perspectives, gender equality, socio-ecological concepts and general riverscape management.

   This book would not have been possible without many helping hands, all of whom it is not pos-
sible to mention by name here. We would like to express our gratitude to Marielza Oliveira (former
Director of the UNESCO Beijing Office), Shahbaz Khan (present Director of the UNESCO Beijing
Office) and Philippe Pypaert (UNESCO Programme Specialist for Natural Sciences), and through
them the UNESCO Beijing Staff who contributed to making the Great Rivers Forum possible. We
wish to thank Mrs Shamila Nair Bedouelle, Assistant Director-General of UNESCO and Mr Abou
Amani, Director of the UNESCO Water Sciences Division, who welcomed and supported this pub-
lication as an inspiration for the Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme of UNESCO to pay
more attention to "Water Culture". Rebecca Tharme (Riverfutures) has kindly revised the quality
of the chapters as the Scientific Reader for this book.
   All authors have taken a great effort to deliver high-class contributions, which were often the first
collaborations between natural and social scientists. They have exceeded their personal limits, under
the severe living and working conditions during the COVID crisis, with all its challenges.
   And finally, personally, I would like to thank my wife Mareike and my family for their untiring
patience and help during the becoming of this book.


Dedication to the late Prof. Dr. Brij Gopal
This book is dedicated to the late Prof. Dr. Brij
Gopal. Brij contributed substantially to the gen-
esis of this book and, given his great interest in
the culture of the River Ganga, would have en-
joyed seeing it come to fruition. The scientific
world has lost one of its brightest minds in river
sciences, and one of the strongest and most ded-
icated supporters of freshwater research in the
Global South, the President of India's National
Institute of Ecology, and the Founder-Coordina-
tor of the Centre for Inland Waters in South Asia.
   Brij touched the personal and professional
lives of the many people with whom he worked
tirelessly for a better future for the planet's rivers
and wetlands. He sadly passed away on 4th Jan                    Fig. 3 Prof. Dr. Brij Gopal at the inauguration of the

2 Reflecting Waters – A Photographer's Reflection



Parolin, Pia

CNRS UMR ISA, INRAE, University of Côte Azur, Sophia Antipolis, France




The photographing of River Cultures (sensu Wantzen et al. 2016) is a way of expressing how humans
and water belong together. And through photography, we can memorize what the rivers tell us.
Photography is visual communication, built on ephemerality and instant transmission, that delivers
a memory (Townsend 2020). Creating visual memories helps us to understand how people lived and
still live on the riverbanks of many rivers around the globe. The photographs and the light games on
the rivers touch our souls. They induce us to remember, visualize, and think.
Who has never enjoyed the inner calm that radiates from a mirror-smooth water surface? From the
tall forest trees reflected on the peaceful water of a river?




 Fig. 2.1 Reflecting light games on the water. All photos by Pia Parolin

                                                                jects. It makes me happy to sit in a boat on a river,
                                                                to cross a huge floodplain, to enjoy the beauty of
                                                                wetlands. If only my reflections could contribute
                                                                to preserve more of these important ecosystems.

                                                       Summary

The Nile, the longest river of the world, connects Northeast Africa from its headwaters near Lake
Victoria to the Mediterranean Sea. This chapter focuses on the Nile in Egypt, where the river's an-
nual inundation (until the building of the two modern dams at Aswan) was the source of the coun-
try's fecundity and guarantor of its civilization since the 6th millennium BCE. While the historical
population of Egypt remained at a maximum of c. four million people until the mid-19th century
when Vice-Roy Muhammad Ali modernized the country, in 2019 the number passed the thresh-
old of 100 million people. Increased demographic pressure, the alteration of the country's ecology
through the mega-impact of the construction of the Aswan High Dam, and industrialization have
led to a massive transformation of the Nile River system. One of the consequences has been an al-
most complete extinction of the country's native fauna and flora. The overuse of the water (rice and
cotton irrigation projects) and the absence of the river's historical natural sedimentation have had
irreversible effects on Egypt's agriculture and heritage (salination; disappearance of archaeological
sites) and caused land loss to rising sea levels in the delta. In view of the environmental degrada-
tion in the Nile valley, and the dangers to Egypt's water security posed by overpopulation and the
construction of the Merowe dams in Sudan and the Renaissance dam in Ethiopia, sustainable water
management is of critical importance.

4.5.1.1 Historical influence of the Nile on
         Egyptian Culture
Human occupation became concentrated along
the Nile Delta, River Valley, and desert oases
during the 5th and especially 4th millennium BCE
when seasonal rains decreased, lessening the
habitability of the desert (see historical over-
view in section 4.3; for discussion of soil ero-
sion and decreasing habitability of the wadis,
see Bunbury 2019). With this shift towards the
Nile River came the adoption of more perma-
nent and densely settled communities, as well
as changes in subsistence livelihoods, such as
the development of irrigation strategies and the
adoption of flood recession agriculture (Bun-

5 The Senegal River, a Disturbed Lifeline in the Sahel



Taïbi, Aude N.1, Kane, Alioune2, Bourlet, Mélanie3, Lorin, Marie3, Ballouche, Aziz4

1
   CNRS UMR ESO, University of Angers, Angers, France
2
   Université Cheikh Anta Diop, Dakar, Sénégal
3
   INALCO-CNRS UMR LLACAN, INALCO, Paris, France
4
   UNESCO Chair River Culture, and CNRS UMR LETG, University of Angers, Angers, France


                                                     Summary

The Senegal River running through the arid and semi-arid parts of Senegal, Mauritania and Mali
is of vital importance in this West African region. Multi-ethnic and multicultural populations have
always been deeply dependent on its ecosystems and water for subsistence economies based on fish-
ing, agriculture and livestock. Called the lifeline of the region, the Senegal River valley has experi-
enced the earliest West African kingdoms as well as French colonization from 1624 onward, with the
first French trading center at the river mouth remaining until independence in 1960. In hydrological
terms, the Senegal River connects the humid upper parts of its valley with the drier basin area of its
lower course, reflecting a strong climatological gradient that strongly affects biological and cultural
diversity.
After serious climatic changes, first apparent in 1968, that have devastated the entire valley, the
riparian states of Mali, Mauritania, Senegal and later, Guinea, decided to join forces to master the
availability of water and seek ways for rational and coordinated exploitation of natural resources.
However, the river regulation infrastructure built (Manantali and Diama dams, dikes and other
irrigation schemes) have had unforeseen environmental and socio-economical consequences along
the Senegal River valley and the estuary. Among the impacts, salinization of soils, degradation of
vegetation, the disappearance of native animal and plant species, diseases, the vanishing of some
economic and socio-cultural activities and rural exodus, are the most important. Different protected
areas have been created since the 1960s, all along the river, in part to reduce these negative impacts.
However, the Senegal River currently remains a disturbed lifeline in the Sahel. Elements of the tra-
ditional cultural use of the river and respect for nature may contribute to the improvement of hydro-
logical and hydro-agricultural schemes.

6 Traditional Use on the Niger River in Mali: Past Knowledge, the
     Current Situation and Future Options



Berton, Jean-Pierre1, Bala, Raita1, Coulibaly, Baba2, Wantzen, Karl M.1, 3

1
   CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, France

   UNESCO Chair River Culture, CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, and CNRS

                                                      Summary

The Niger River is the third-largest African river. Its valley in West Africa is situated between the
drier Sahel zone in the North and the equatorial rain forest to the South, forming a climatologi-
cal, biogeographical and cultural transition zone, which is one of the cradles of humanity. Climatic
phases of wetter and drier years have caused migrations and cultural exchanges. Its valley is char-
acterized by the existence of several socio-cultural groups distributed among specific geographical
and cultural areas. This chapter focuses on specific cultural use forms of the river that the Niger
basin is famous for, with a strong focus on navigation, but also about fisheries and transhumance
pastoralism. All these traditional use forms undergo a recent transformation and a loss of biocultural
diversity. The Niger has still maintained its characteristic flow regime, although the existing dams,
combined with intensive water withdrawal for agriculture, strongly influence the low water season.
The dynamics of its delta are still active, but oil spills and other impacts threaten the high biological
diversity. Recently, diverse initiatives have gathered perspectives and information to face the chal-
lenges of resource management and development potential of this unique river.

   More recently, the use of sawn planks and
synthetic fiber ropes has resulted in more hy-
drodynamic forms and greater safety. The canoe
adapted to powerful engines are now called pi-
nasses. They have considerably increased in size,
and the rear rostrum (kouloupala) made a place
for outboarders or rear rudders. Today, most
pinasses are completely nailed, making them
tighter and stiffer but more vulnerable in case
of accidents. Some of them are equipped with
an upper deck, sheltered from a coachroof, real
masterpieces of the artisanal shipyards of Mopti
(Viguier 2008).
   The construction of wooden canoes is only
possible if the physical characteristics of natu-
ral materials are thoroughly known. The wood
choice and the period when to cut trees are de-
cisive to achieve its maximal durability. Part of
this know-how remains secret. It is not the pre-
rogative of an ethnic group, but the Bozos have a
de facto supremacy over the technology. Songs,
myths, and legends often trade this knowledge.
   According to Ligers (1969: 99–100), "It is
known that a canoe made of kaïcédrat boards reach-
es a life of twenty years, and that made of tamarind
planks only three or four years; the ebony wood Dio-
spyros mespiliformis or the Mystragyna inermis also
provide good boards, much better than those of a bao-
bab Adansonia digitata, a rônier Borassus flabellifer,
an Acacia albida, or Shea Butyrosperum parkii, the
latter being still superior to those of a cheese-trees,
or a ficus". The same author reports that "in the
spirit of the builders of canoes, in Nouh for example
(the Nouhoun-bozo) the important thing is to choose a
'good wood': if the cut tree belonged to a wicked jinn,
the canoe built with its boards would not be excellent,
and the owner of this boat will always be pursued by
bad luck; on the contrary, if you come across a tree
that has a good jinn, the boat will bring a lot of money    Fig. 6.5 Traditional boat architecture on the Niger River

7 The Sanaga River, an Example of Biophysical and Socio-Cultural
     Integration in Cameroon, Central Africa



Zébazé Togouet, Serge H.1, Nyamsi Tchatcho, Narcisse2, Tharme, Rebecca E.3, 4,
Piscart, Christophe5

1
   University of Yaoundé 1, Faculty of Science, Laboratory of Hydrobiology and Environment,
    Yaoundé, Cameroon
2
   University of Douala, Institute of Fisheries Sciences, Laboratory of Ecosystem Management,
    Douala, Cameroon
3
   Riverfutures, Cressbrook, Buxton, Derbyshire, UK
4
   Le Studium Loire Valley Institute for Advanced Studies, Orléons, France
5
   University of Rennes 1, Laboratoire Écosystèmes Biodiversité Évolution, CNRS UMR 6553
    ECOBIO, Rennes, France


                                                    Summary

The Sanaga River is the largest in Cameroon and one of the main resources for the economic de-
velopment of the country. A lack of electricity is one of the primary setbacks for the Cameroonian
economy, and the national authorities plan to at least double, from 2,000 MW, the nation's hydro-
power electricity supply by 2035. Representing more than 75% of the estimated total hydro potential
of Cameroon, the Sanaga River has one of the greatest hydropower potentials in Africa. As well as
being a vital asset for the national economy, it possesses exceptional natural features such as water-
falls, biodiversity hotspots with endemic and rare wildlife (e.g., the West African manatee, hippo-
potamus, chimpanzee and forest elephant), and very high cultural diversity, with numerous ethnic
groups represented. There are many human activities along the river (use of water resources for
food security and irrigated agriculture, inland fisheries, intensive aquaculture, sand extraction and
hydropower production) that are increasing, and with visibly detrimental effects. The construction
of dams has forced the local population to move from one livelihood activity to another. The unique
cultural heritage and biodiversity are hence under pressure, due to over-fishing, logging, hunting,
agrochemical pollution and habitat destruction. Unfortunately, the management actions necessary
for remediation of these detrimental impacts are not well captured in basin development plans. It is
therefore considered urgent to implement more sustainable human activities, including the develop-
ment of alternative economic resources, such as ecotourism.

Bala, Raita1, Wantzen, Karl M.1, 2

      Strasbourg, Strasbourg, France



                                                   Summary

Since ancient times, human civilization is linked to rivers, and these rivers maintain our lives like
blood vessels. The Congo River connects Central Africa and its primary forest to the Atlantic Ocean
and has been used as the main commercial route for centuries till today. More than 75 million people
and a unique fauna and flora live in the equatorial forest and countries of its basin. The Congo has
(yet) faced fewer human impacts than other rivers of the same size; the most significant ones are the
construction of small dams on its tributaries and two big dams on the lower part of the Congo River,
but further large dams are planned for hydropower generation and inter-basin water transfer, with
yet unfathomed socio-ecological consequences. Since the past two decades, there is an increase in
plastic waste in the Congo River. The main reason behind that change is the lack of waste manage-
ment systems and water treatment plants in all cities located on its banks, that is the case of Kinshasa,
the capital city of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), the third-largest megalopolis in
Africa, Brazzaville the capital city of the Republic of Congo, or other big cities like Matadi. Mining
and deforestation are spreading in the entire basin. Congo is not just a river that crosses entire central
Africa; it is also the mother, the identity, and the symbol of patriotism for people who live in its basin
and depend on all the resources it gives. Even the population of urban areas depends on its resources
and uses the river as the main route for supplying goods in different areas. From its source to its es-
tuary, the Congo River does not only transport sediments; it also carries myths, stories, legends, and
fables about its origins, the entities that haunt it, and forces that animate it. This River is a source of
life, it fertilizes lands, fulfills the needs of all living creatures, and maintains the global equilibrium.

Each of the about 17 empires or kingdoms of
the Congo Basin was subdivided into differ-
ent chiefdoms (57 in total), and each of those
was composed of several ethnic groups. Today,
DR Congo alone is home to more than 250 ethnic
groups (Globalsecurity.org 2015).
   At the coastal zone of the Mayombe forest,
people were attracted by copper, lead, and iron.
At around 400, Bantu-speakers settled on the
north and the south of the Upper Congo. From
the 2nd to 15th century, the region witnessed an
increase in population; it was also due to mi-
grations of other Bantu-speakers from the east
(­
 UNESCO 1992). Later, they organized them-
selves into smalls kingdoms such as the Ka-
kongo, Ngoyo, and Loango kingdoms that later
merged into the Kongo kingdom.
   The Kongo Kingdom was recorded for the
first time in the 15th century by the Portuguese.

                                                     Summary

The Mara River starts its journey in the Mau forest in Kenya, flowing through diverse waterscapes
and famous savannahs into Tanzania, where it reaches the Mara wetland system before spilling
into Lake Victoria. The Mara River is a crucial river of East Africa, as it is part of the Nile Basin
(which it feeds through Lake Victoria). The landscapes surrounding the Mara River are shaped by
the seasonality of its flows. Its exceptional flora and fauna follow the rhythm of water availability,
and human inhabitants have adapted to and influenced the ecosystem services provided by the
local environment. For millennia and more intensively in the past centuries, different peoples have
been inspired by the river ecosystem to give meaning, and create culture and livelihoods adapted
to their environment. In the Mau forest where the Mara River starts its journey, the Ogieks have
been protecting trees providing sources to the river; in the savannahs of the current Maasai Mara
and Serengeti national park, Maasai people have been living in harmony with wildlife, adopting a
nomadic lifestyle; in the Wetlands of the Mara, fishing communities regulate practice rituals linked
to the particular landscape of the lower Mara.
   However, threats to the Mara River have been increasing and affecting the quality and quantity
of river flows. Climate change, colonization, land tenure changes, intensification of agricultural and
fishing methods, increased human pollution, and a lack of governance are some of the main causes
of the degradation of the river. Current efforts are addressing governance, improving the monitor-
ing of flows and allocation of water, with the objective of improving the environmental, economic
and social sustainability of the Mara River Basin. There is much benefit in learning from the adaptive
ways in which peoples inhabiting the basin for millennia have built resilience to the surrounding
ecosystem.

10 A Tail-End Tale: The Story of the Indus Delta



Raza, Syeda M.1, Aslam, Mariyam2, Vazhayil, Alvin M.2

1
     University of Rochester, Rochester, NY, United States
2
     CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, France



                                                     Summary

The Indus is one of the most important global river systems, and it has played a significant role in de-
veloping civilization in Asia. It serves as a lifeline in the Indian subcontinent, especially in Pakistan.
However, the river has been subjected to various anthropogenic stresses, including structural inter-
ventions at different points, overexploitation of the ecosystem, and pollution. The most affected re-
gion of the basin is the Indus Delta, the tail-end section of the river system, due to the construction of
the Kotri Barrage and subsequent reductions in the flow of water and sediments downstream. These
interventions have reduced the area of the delta and have put the unique mangrove forests at stake.
This chapter analyzes the distinctive cultural, biological, and historical features of the river system
in the deltaic region, focusing on the Thatta district on the east and the Badin district west of the
riverbank in Sindh province, Pakistan. We examine human-river relationships and their reciprocity
with habits and habitats in the delta, such as the unusual transcendence of religious boundaries be-
tween the Hindus and Muslims by virtue of their shared spiritual connections with the river. We also
underline the importance of protecting riverine ecosystems and conserving the rich cultures they
help foster. The chapter then recommends region-specific management suggestions such as policy
changes and the utilization of religious and folklore elements to halt further degradation and help
revive the Indus Delta.

 Famous elements of               It is the only habitat for the Indus River dolphins (Platanista minor). The grey
 biodiversity                     and white mangroves of the Indus Delta are uniquely resistant to extreme
                                  conditions.

 Famous elements of culture       Present-day communities in Sindh derive their roots from the Indus Valley
                                  Civilization. Hence, the river's influence is seen in the cultural and daily
                                  practices, including architecture, livelihood, and spiritual activities. The Palla
                                  fish is deemed essential in Sindhi folklore. Indigenous communities live on
                                  the river and rely heavily on fishing. Moreover, the country's dependence on
                                  the River for power and irrigation makes it the backbone of the economy and
                                  society.

   By 1514, the Portuguese had taken control of
Sindh (Holdich 1911), and due to its high-quality
exports via the port, Thatta became one of the
wealthiest cities in the world (Markovits 2000).
In 1526, the Mughal Empire was established in
the Indian subcontinent, and by 1592, the Mu-
ghals had gained control in Sindh. This event
happened during the reign of Akbar, who was
intent on capturing Thatta's seaports to create
maritime networks with Arabia and Persia and
guard the region against the Portuguese. During
this period, Thatta also became a center for the
ship-building industry; in fact, it has been doc-
umented that the chief (Sarkar) of Thatta alone
owned 40,000 boats, denoting the importance of
Thatta's riverine trade. Eventually, this trade de-
clined due to siltation that blocked the port and
changed the course of the Indus (Shah 2016), and
so, Thatta's importance diminished (Markovits
2000).

   The legend of Jhulelal (fig. 10.7) revolves
around the Indus. He is also known as Zinda
Pir ('living saint'), or Uderolal in Hindu com-
munities, and Shaikh Tahir/Khawaja Khizar
amongst Muslims (Albinia 2010). As the legend
goes, during the rule of Mirkshah – who would
forcibly convert his Hindu subjects to Islam – the
Sindhi Hindus prayed to Varuna (the river God)
at the Indus banks for 40 days. They were prom-
ised a savior in the form of the reincarnation of
Varuna, and so, Jhulelal was born and is said to
have confronted Mirkshah, saying, "He whom you
call Allah, and my people call Krishna are the same!"
   In another tale, he shocked the court with wa-
ter-related miracles to prove the legitimacy of his
divine powers. As a wave of water hovered above
Mirkshah and fire encircled the court, the rul-
er begged Jhulelal for forgiveness. Jhulelal then
asked the Hindus to construct a temple in com-
memoration of the event and instructed them al-          Fig. 10.7 Jhulelal Statue, Happy Valley Hindu Temple.
ways to have water available for "daat" (holy sip).      Photo: thetempletrail, Flickr, CC BY-ND 2.0

11 Yamuna: A Goddess in Distress



Vazhayil, Alvin M.1, Wantzen, Karl M.1, 2

1
     CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, France
2
     UNESCO Chair River Culture, University of Tours, Tours, and CNRS UMR LIVE, University of
      Strasbourg, Strasbourg, France



                                                  Summary

The Yamuna is considered one of the holiest rivers in the Indian subcontinent. The river is a part of
India's history, dating back to the Mahabharata era (1450 BC), the Indus valley civilization, and the
Mughal era of the 17th century. The river has been a symbol of spirituality and nobility. However,
the river has been facing severe environmental degradation since the past century. The country's
rapid development and industrial revolution have exerted tremendous pressure on the river basin,
with the river's 22 km stretch through the National Capital Territory of Delhi being heavily pollut-
ed. The disposal of untreated or partly treated industrial and sewage effluents, the inefficiency of
the sewage treatment plants, agricultural activities, canalization, and diversion of water to meet the
growing population's needs in the lower segments has led to the present devastating state of the riv-
er. Although the upper segments are comparatively cleaner and healthier, overgrazing and urban-
ization threaten the basin's biodiversity. Even when the Yamuna is a center of attraction for spiritual
activities, the river is exploited with devotees disposing of offerings, dead bodies, mass bathings,
and over-tourism. Such activities have degraded the riverine biodiversity, especially in the plains,
with many species endangered or extinct. Steps to ensure the protection of riverine ecosystems like
Ramsar sites, biodiversity parks, and natural sewage treatment plants to improve the river's biotic
features are positive signs. Various NGOs and religious groups do their part by spreading aware-
ness through festivals and rituals, educating the public to reduce plastics and non-biodegradable
materials harmful to aquatic life.

 Length (km)           1,376
 Mean [min/max]        Average about 2,950 Min: 99.1,Max: 23,446.34 (Hathnikund Barrage)
 annual discharge
 (m3 s-1)
 Hydrological          The primary source of water – southwest monsoon (June–September)
 pattern               Minimum discharge period – winter season (October–February)
 Degree of             The river is profoundly disturbed in the lower basin and the plains with human
 naturalness           impacts. Flow is regulated with barrages, diverted and canalized from the upper
                       segment until the Delhi segment
 Natural               The topography is divided into three – Hilly and Tarai region (3.19%, Uttar Pradesh,
 landscape types       Himachal Pradesh, Uttarkhand), foothills and plateaus (44%, Madhya Pradesh,
                       Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh), plains and valleys (47.22%, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh,
                       Rajasthan, and Haryana)
                       The upper Yamuna catchment falls into three physiographic belts – Lesser Himalayas,
                       Siwaliks, and the Doon valley. The basin is fan-shaped till the river comes to the plain,
                       i.e., upstream of Tajewala barrage.
 Impact types          Barrages – The Yamuna has six barrages along its first 700 km stretch. Three of them are
                       located in Delhi (Wazirabad, I.T.O., and Okhla). Three more (Katapathar, Panipat, and
                       Agra barrages) are under discussion.
                        Canals – The river is diverted at Tajewala by western and eastern canals. The river foes
                       down 280 km to Okhla from where the Agra canal begins.
                       A hydel project completed in the Tons River in 1972, and another one is under
                       consideration at Kaishu since the 1960s
 Largest cities        Delhi (18.98 million), Agra (1.586 million), Allahabad (1.113 million)
 (inhabitants)
 Urbanization          Urbanization in the Ganga-Yamuna basin dates back to the 1st BC. It was later
                       intensified with the arrival of the Mughals in Delhi. In the 19th and 20th centuries, the
                       colonial period saw embankments' construction and the river's taming.
                       The urban population has almost doubled during the last two decades (2001–2011),
                       and the number of cities and towns increased by 21%. The overall increase in the states'
                       urban population in the Yamuna basin is 90% in the last two decades.
                       Land use and land cover change under settlements increased by 186.5% between 1970
                       and 2002.
 Protected areas       (1) Surajpur wetland is an urban wetland in the Yamuna basin at 184.7 m asl. The area
                       is a reserve forest and spreads across 308 ha, of which 60 ha are natural wetlands. The
                       wetland supports diverse threatened flora and fauna, including 186 species of birds
                       belonging to 44 families, 6 mammals, 15 species of fishes, 52 species of butterflies, and
                       more than 200 plants.
                       (2) The Yamuna Biodiversity Park – Located near Wazirabad village. Spreads over an
                       area of 9,770 ha protecting the river and Aravalli hills. It consists of heritage sites and is
                       home to 50 threatened communities in the basin. Two wetlands, grasslands, and forest
                       communities have been developed in the park. 60% of the area is projected to be under
                       wetland marshes.

 of culture               the origin point of the river, the Yamunotri shrine, Poanta Shahib Gurudwara, Sangam,

12 The Mekong: Death of a River Culture?



Campbell, Ian

Rhithroecology Pty Ltd., Victoria, Australia


                                                   Summary

The Mekong is possibly one of the most disputed rivers worldwide. The ever-increasing number of
dams is controlling flow and reducing the sediment load to a minimal percentage, resulting in that
millennia-old cultures depending on the fertile floods, and millions of people directly living on the
natural resources gained from the flooding are at risk. The Mekong Delta, one of the most important
biodiversity hotspots of the world, is shrinking, as it receives a mere 1% of the pre-dam sediment in-
put. This paper makes a plea for reinforcing the international efforts of the countries the river crosses
(China, Myanmar, Lao, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam) for restoring the social and ecological
baselines necessary for a sustainable development of the Mekong basin.

The Mekong: Death of a River Culture?                                                                        269


are washed downstream as they develop, with
some being transported up the Tonle Sap River
during the reversal of flow. The larvae grow and
develop on the inundated flood plains, includ-
ing the inundated flooded forest surrounding
Tonle Sap Great Lake. As the flood recedes the
grown fish migrate back to the river channels
and recommence their breeding migration, a be-
havior which is exploited by fishers, most nota-
bly by the dai fishery in the Tonle Sap River in
the vicinity of Phnom Penh.
   Many aquatic insects have their emergence
and reproduction during the low flow period
including mayflies such as Ephemera species, dy-
tiscid beetles and giant water bugs (Lethocerus
species, fig. 12.7). The slower current speeds at
that time make emergence easier, and eggs and
newly hatched larvae are less likely to be washed
away and less constrained by the reduced habi-
tat area during the dry period.

12.4.2 Fish and Rice
The flood pulse of the Mekong has played a key
role supporting the two key biological resources
of the basin: fish and rice (figs. 12.5, 12.6). There
are two features of the fish of the Mekong Basin.
The first is the extraordinary diversity of fish
species, and the second is the very high produc-
tivity of the fishery. The high diversity appears
to have arisen largely due to stream 'capture'
(retrograde erosion ending up in the connection
of two watersheds) by the proto-Mekong River
(Carling 2009, Rainboth 1996). Two separate river
systems, one flowing to the Gulf of Thailand and
the other flowing to the South China Sea evolved
distinctive fish faunas, but the stream flowing to
the South China Sea 'captured' the headwaters of
the other stream, together with its fish fauna.
   The flood pulse of the river, and the exten-
sive alluvial floodplain, resulted in vast areas of
warm, shallow, nutrient-rich water which sup-
ported, and continue to support, the growth and
reproduction of fish and other aquatic animals.
This floodplain is most extensive in Cambodia
and includes the flooded forest area surround-
ing the Tonle Sap Great Lake, and extensive ar-
eas around Phnom Penh and down into the del-
ta. Shallow waters inundating rich alluvial soils
are nutrient-rich, supporting high phytoplank-
ton production which feeds invertebrates and
fish, which in turn support people.
   The flood pulse also provided ideal conditions
for growing rice. Rice is a key component of the        Fig. 12.7 Above: Light traps set up to collect aquatic
diets of the people of the Lower Mekong, to the         insects along stream channels near Tonle Sap Great lake

rectly as the flood rose or receded (recession rice)
or the flood was used to fill dams that were used
to irrigate rice fields once the flood had receded.
Having large areas of fertile gently sloping flood-
plain, as exists in the Mekong, allows the cultiva-
tion of large areas of rice, and thus a large crop.

13 River Culture in China and India, a Comparative Perspective on
       its Origins, Challenges, and Applications



Cao, Yixin1, Vazhayil, Alvin M.1

 CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, France
1




         "Do you not see the Yellow River come from the sky, rushing into the sea and never come back?"
              (In Chinese: 君不见，黄河之水天上来，奔流到海不复回。出自李白《将进酒)
                                                               Li Bai, Chinese poet in the Tang Dynasty (618 to 907 CE)



    "Rivers do not drink their water; trees do not eat their fruit; clouds do not swallow their rain. What great
                                  ones have is always for the benefit of others."
                                                                                                       Hindu Proverb



                                                    Summary

India and China are huge, neighboring Asian countries that bear the largest populations and the old-
est traditions about rivers – the deep-rooted "Mother"/"God" river identity makes rivers the cradle of
ancient civilizations in both cultures. We make an effort to synthesize their common features based
on the River Culture Concept. This chapter is divided into three aspects: (I) how and why the bio-cul-
tural River Culture in China and India are currently in danger; (II) how are they (or could be) saved
in favor of a sustainable management; (III) provide examples of different measures to improve the
socio-ecological integrity of rivers. We found that both Chinese and Indian rivers are experiencing
rapid industrialization and urbanization at the cost of severe physical-chemical degradation of their
rivers. China has an extremely high degree of river fragmentation due to intensive dam building
and land-use change, a leap after the 1978 economic reform. In India, the river flow and human-in-
duced changes of the river channels emerged in the colonial period, and Indian rivers suffer from
heavy pollution in urban and rural areas due to limited sewage treatment capacity. Today, India and
China promote ecological river restoration as a sustainability strategy under the pressure of global
warming threats, carbon emission commitment, and the cross-border dispute over water resources.

River Culture in China and India                                                                                    285


    Being a metaphor for permanent change and
eternity, the hydrological cycle, which is well
represented by the increasing discharge of river
systems, has inspired philosophers of all kinds.
Using "water" as a metaphor of "constant flux"
to illustrate dialectics' ideas played a vital role in
Daoism and Confucianism. Such as Confucius:
"The passage of time is just like the flow of the river,
which goes on day and night." In the concept of Yin-
Yang, water is considered to be quintessentially
yin, a symbol of "the yielding, receptive, feminine,
and dark aspects of nature". The metaphor appeared
in several places in Daode Jing (in Chinese: ­道德
经) is a classic of Chinese philosophical literature
written by the 6th century BC sage Lao-Tse/Laozi:
"Nothing in the world is softer than water", "The soft
overcomes the hard, and the gentle overcomes the ag-
gressive" (Salguero 2017). The characteristics of
water are utilized to present certain moral char-
acters: modest, selfless, generous, etc., such as
Laozi: "The highest goodness is like water. Water bene-
fits all things and does not compete. It stays in the low-
ly places which others despise." and Confucius: "The
wise find pleasure in water; the virtuous find pleasure
in hills. The wise are active; the virtuous are tran-
quil. The wise are joyful; the virtuous are long-lived."
Moreover, the word "eternity" in Chinese is "永",
which means "permanent." "永" was written as
in Oracle bone script (ancestor of modern Chinese
characters), and the pictogram was originally de-
rived from the shape of flowing rivers.

                                                    Summary

The Yangtze River is the largest river in China. It runs across the central part of China, with a total
length of more than 6,300 km, it is the third-largest river in the world after the Nile and Amazon.
Along with the Yellow River, the Yangtze River can be seen as the mother river of the Chinese na-
tion. There are multiple cultural areas in the Yangtze River basin, and these distinctive regional cul-
tures have contributed to the construction of the harmony in diversity pattern of the Yangtze River
Basin and even the whole Chinese culture. About 1000 years ago, the Yangtze River Basin officially
replaced the Yellow River Basin as China's economic and cultural center. Since modern times, the
Yangtze River has become an essential channel for western academic introduction into China, lead-
ing China to gradually move from traditional to modern and is still the forerunner of Chinese cul-
tural development. The Yangtze River Basin has a diverse topography, complex climatic conditions,
and a unique natural environment. It has developed plateaus, mountains and rivers in the upper
reaches, river networks, lakes, wetlands and floodplains in the middle and lower reaches, and salt
and fresh water wetlands at the river mouth. It is one of the hot spots of biodiversity globally and
one of the most important freshwater ecosystems in China. However, the ecological environment
of the Yangtze River Basin is currently threatened by multiple factors. This has attracted the great
attention of the Chinese government. A movement has been launched to improve the conservation
of the Yangtze River and halt unsustainable development.

                                                     a       14.3. Historical introduction
                                                             Early ancestors of human beings have been
                                                             found in the Yangtze River Basin, including some
                                                             6.2 million-year-old skulls from Lufengpithecus
                                                             lufengensis, from Lufeng County, Yunnan Prov-
                                                             ince, on the upper reaches of the Yangtze Riv-
                                                             er (Chang et al. 2015). In addition, the fossil of
                                                             Yuanmou Man, about 1.7 million years ago, rep-
                                                             resents the oldest known Homo erectus in China
                                                             (Qi et al. 2006). Since the 1930s, many Neolith-
                                                             ic cultural sites have been found in the Yangtze
                                                             River Basin. Many highly developed prehistoric
                                                             civilizations had emerged there, and the most
                                b
                                                             famous of which are Sanxingdui Culture (about
                                                             4,800–2,600 BP) (Gao and Guo 2016) in the upper
                                                             reaches, Shijiahe Culture (about 4,600–4,000 BP)
                                                             (Liu and Zhang 2013) in the middle reaches,
                                                             Hemudu culture (about 7,000–5,300 BP) and
                                                             Liangzhu Cultures (about 5,300–4,200 BP) (Liu
                                                             2001) in the lower reaches. At that time, the peo-
                                                             ple in many areas of the Yangtze River Basin
                                                             lived an agricultural life of rice planting. Their
                                                             handicraft industry was very developed, pro-
                                                             ducing the earliest lacquerware and silk in China
                                                             and making significant contributions to human
                                                             civilization.
                                                                After entering the dynastic era (about 2,100–
                                                             1600 BC), the civilization of the Yangtze River
                                                     c       Basin was firstly impacted by wars and floods.
                                                             Its economic and cultural development was
                                                             slow, and its level of technology and living
                                                             condition was far less developed than that of
                                                             the Yellow River Basin in the north. However,
                                                             its unique economy and culture were develop-
                                                             ing fast. In the Shang Dynasty (from the early
                                                             16th century BC to the mid 11th century BC), the
                                                             development of bronzes in the Yangtze Riv-
                                                             er Basin accelerated, and cultural areas such as
                                                             Sanxingdui in the upper reaches, Panlongcheng
                                                             in the middle reaches, Wucheng and Maqiao in
                                                             the lower reaches appeared. In the Zhou Dynas-
                                                     d       ty (from the middle of the 11th century BC to the
                                                             end of the 3rd century BC), the economy and cul-
                                                             ture of the Yangtze River Basin continued to de-
                                                             velop and began to blend with foreign cultures,
                                                             forming three major cultural areas: Bashu in the
                                                             upper reaches, ­  Jingchu in the middle reaches
                                                             and Wuyue in the lower reaches. The three cul-
                                                             tural areas had close exchanges and influences
                                                             and absorbed much cultural nourishment from
                                                             the Yellow River Basin in the north. Generally
                                                             speaking, the culture of the Yangtze River in the

15 China's Grand Canal: An Eco-Cultural Community connecting
       Five River Systems



Zhang, Tinghao1, Yu, Bing1, Wan, Jinhong2

1
     Chinese Academy of Cultural Heritage, Beijing, China
2
     China Institute of Water Resources and Hydropower Research, Beijing, China



                                                         Summary

The Grand Canal, linking five major river systems, is a unique joint masterpiece by humans and
nature in Chinese and world history. It is the result of a nation in great need of water, with a special
vision about water, with the capability of solving sophisticated water problems. It is an eco-cultural
synergy, an outstanding representation of the pre-industrial engineering heritage of human beings.
Ancient artificial waterways, still under-represented in considerations about heritage conservation
worldwide, should be better understood establishing the context between engineering as a purpose-
and problem-orientation, with thematics in landscape planning, culture and philosophy. The estab-
lishment of the Grand Canal Cultural Belt program initiated in 2018 will endow the Grand Canal
with new functions and missions to realize creative transformation and development. The apprecia-
tion of its values, from the original transportation and water project to a living cultural heritage, and
eco-cultural synergy, represents the evolution of human-nature relationships.

                                                           nal from natural rivers and lakes and became an
                                                           independent, engineered system. It was also in
                                                           the Song Dynasty when sophisticated facilities
                                                           with multiple engineering functions were cre-
                                                           ated in the Huaiyang and Jiangnan Canals. The
                                                           chambered ship gate was one example which
                                                           was consisted of a pair of gates, diversion and
                                                           retreating channels, and a water storage pond.
                                                           In addition to the seasonal water regulation
                                                           function, the chambered gates had developed
                                                           into a navigation system that was similar to
                                                           modern ship locks which used multi-level gates
                                                           and drainage (return) facilities. The facilities of
                                                           the Milan Locks in the 17th century were almost
                                                           identical with the Zhenzhou Gate in the Song
                                                           dynasty of late 10th century (Kirby et al. 1990).
                                                           Such chambered gates were set up at the mouth
                                                           of the Canal across the Huaihe River, the Yang-
                                                           tze River and the Qiantang River. The main
                                                           technical achievements during this period were
                                                           the relative independence of the canal sections
                                                           connecting the Yangtze River, the Yellow Riv-
                                                           er and the Huaihe River, and the development
                                                           of multiple-function engineering systems. With
                                                           engineering complexes at the river mouths for
                                                           smooth connection of the Canal and natural
                                                           rivers, they also facilitated comprehensive func-
                                                           tions such as traffic dispatch, water supply and
                                                           sediment control, so that the boundary between
                                                           the artificial waterway and the natural rivers be-
                                                           came increasingly distinct. The chambered-gate
                                                           engineering system became the symbol of Chi-
                                                           na's leading water engineering technology at
                                                           that time.

                                                            Broadly speaking, the cultural diversity of the

                                                            evidence can be classified into three categories

                                                    Summary

The management of transboundary rivers is largely affected by multilateral relations, due to con-
cerns on water security and scarcity. The Amur-Heilong River is the largest transboundary river in
northeast Asia and one of the longest free-flowing rivers on Earth, flowing from headwaters in Mon-
golia to China and Russia. The river basin supports high levels of landscape diversity, biodiversity
and rich cultural diversity. However, these diversities have been threatened by intensive human
activities, which lead to gradual degradation. Endemic fish are close to extinction, the landscape has
been transformed, waters are polluted, sediment flows are disturbed, tributaries are dammed, even
the free-flowing main stem is currently threatened by a dam construction plan. Plans to save this
river are urgently needed. Under the Silk Road Economic Belt initiative, the trilateral relationship
between the neighboring countries in the basin is becoming stronger. It increases economic pressure,
but it also gives opportunities for protecting these tremendous natural treasures of the Amur-Hei-
long River Basin, through broader and deeper cooperation between countries of the basin and in-
volvement of local inhabitants. We provide the following suggestions to manage the Amur-Heilong
River Basin in a sustainable way for both inhabitants (cultural diversity) and environments (bio-
diversity): (1) Sustainable use of riverine resources; (2) Develop trilateral cooperative projects and
platforms; (3) Apply nature-based solutions for flood management; (4) Enhance public participation;
(5) Adopt water-saving methods and adjust development plans; and (6) Develop sustainable river
basin economics.

                                                         Summary

The Saskatchewan River Delta (SRD) in western Canada formed over the past 10,000 years, built by
sediment accumulation and carved by river floods, creating a patchwork of geomorphically-diverse
water bodies, each with its own hydrological, biochemical and ecological character. The inland delta
became a wildlife hotspot, and Swampy Cree and Métis people were drawn there to live in rhythm
with water and wildlife. By the late 1800s, more than 100,000 muskrats were harvested each year in
the thriving fur trade. As many or more waterfowl passed through every fall as they migrated along
the North American central flyway. Commercial fisheries for sturgeon and walleye provided income
and food for residents. Yet the past century has brought several changes to the SRD. The human pop-
ulation upstream has grown from less than one million to more than three million, bringing conse-
quent demands for electricity generated from hydropower and irrigation water for food production.
Flows through the SRD have declined and become less predictable. Wildlife population numbers
have dropped. The people of the delta now often feel powerless, because their voices are not heard.
But there are signs of hope. Delta communities are sustaining culture through a resurgence of lan-
guage and on-the-land activities. Knowledge is being handed down to a new generation of delta
stewards. Community leaders are pushing for greater accountability from upstream decision-mak-
ers and are building capacity to recognize and protect this ecologically, economically and culturally
crucial delta.


                                                              17.1 Introduction
                                                              Rivers worldwide face myriad stressors that
                                                              include pollution, invasive species and unsus-
                                                              tainable land-use change and water withdraw-
                                                              als (Vörösmarty et al. 2010). The problems these
                                                              threats present in river basins often manifest
                                                              themselves most strongly in the lower reaches.
                                                              River deltas, which once benefitted from flood
                                                              pulses and sediment supply from upstream, also
                                                              tend to be most vulnerable to loss of these flood
                                                              pulses, disruption of sediment transport, and
                                                              deposition of both organic and inorganic pollut-

                                    melt, the second in July, from melting of the snowpack in the distant Rocky
                                    Mountains
 Degree of naturalness              Incoming flows to the delta are heavily regulated due to the operation of
                                    Brazeau Dam on the North Saskatchewan R., Gardiner Dam on the South
                                    Saskatchewan R., and E.B. Campbell Dam on the Saskatchewan R.
 Natural landscape types            Delta floodplain at the transition between the Great Plains and the Boreal
                                    Forest
 Impact types                       Climate (drought events, flood events; storm events; lost glaciers in
                                    headwaters); ecological impact (high/low sediment flow; natural changes
                                    to waterways; fish and animal habitats); human impact (localized water
                                    control structures; trapping, fishing, and hunting pressure; policy impact
                                    [irrigation expansion upstream; farming runoff impact; jurisdictional/
                                    management impact]).
 Largest cities (inhabitants)       The Pas, Manitoba (pop. 5,513) is the only city in the delta itself. The second
                                    major center is Cumberland House (pop. 1,487), the oldest settlement in
                                    western Canada, established in 1774.
 Urbanization                       Less than 1%
 Protected areas                    Nil

18 The Lower Illinois River, USA: The Interaction of Floodplain
    Culture with Scientific Understanding



Schneider, Daniel

Department of Urban and Regional Planning, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign,
Champaign, IL, USA


                                                  Summary

The backwater lakes and wetlands of the lower Illinois River floodplain were historically one of the
great natural resources of the state of Illinois, USA. Up until the beginning of the 20th century, they
supported a diverse regional economy based on fishing, hunting, logging, recreation, navigation and
agriculture. Starting around the turn of the century, however, the floodplain was disconnected from
the river by artificial levees, for flood control and the backwater lakes were drained, for agriculture.
By 1920, over half of the floodplain had been drained for agriculture. At that time, residents of the
Illinois River valley understood the role of the flood pulse and its benefits for fish, wildlife and veg-
etation in the river and its floodplain. This local knowledge helped inform early scientists, such as
Stephen Forbes, in their foundational studies of the ecology of the flood pulse. Conflicts over rights
to lands, waters, and resources influenced the shape of the floodplain and relations between locals
and scientists. Following severe flooding and the resultant economic damage in 1993, land managers
began to use concepts of the flood pulse in river-floodplain restoration activities.

   Forbes and the other scientists at the Illinois        connected their ecological work to the growing
State Laboratory of Natural History (now called           political efforts to protect the fishery.
                                                              Beginning in 1876, while he was investigating
                                                          the food habits of the fishes, Forbes worked with
                                                          local fishermen on the Illinois, Ohio and Missis-
                                                          sippi rivers. These 'bottom-landers' – fishermen,
                                                          hunters and boatmen – were central players
                                                          in the scientific enterprise of the station. They
                                                          worked as field assistants, guiding scientists in
                                                          unfamiliar locations. They helped the scientists
                                                          as laborers, rowing boats and collecting fish in
                                                          their seines, trammel nets and fish traps. They
                                                          provided more than manual labor, however;
                                                          they provided knowledge, both on how to catch
                                                          fish and on their natural history. As these fisher-
                                                          men had developed the techniques of working
                                                          on the river over many decades of practice, their
                                                          gear was highly suited to the conditions on the
                                                          Illinois River and its floodplain. They used a va-
                                                          riety of nets and fish traps, and developed boats
                                                          that could navigate with heavy loads of fish on
                                                          the often shallow and weed-choked backwaters.
                                                          As scientists discovered that the fishing tech-
                                                          niques they brought from other areas were not
                                                          effective, they adopted those techniques of the
                                                          local fishermen.
                                                              Fishermen also taught the scientists about
                                                          the natural history of the different fish species.

19 The Trinity River in Texas – Muddy and Emblematic



Klaver, Irene, J.1, Hoeinghaus, David J.2, Grossman, Jacob W.1, Frith, Aaron J.1, Atkinson,
Samuel F.2, Kennedy, James H.2

1
     University of North Texas, Department of Philosophy and Religion, Denton, TX, USA
2
     University of North Texas, Department of Biological Sciences, Denton, TX, USA



                                                      Summary

The Trinity River is a muddy, rather unassuming river. It is no Nile, Ganges, Amazon, Mississippi,
or Rhine. Still, it supports two of the largest population centers in the United States and its trajectory
through time is emblematic of many a river. For thousands of years, the active land-water dynamics
shapeshifted the area, Indigenous peoples adjusted accordingly. From the early 19th century this
changed drastically, when Anglo-American colonists settled along the river, growing cotton, raising
cattle, building cities. Human-land dynamics began to shape the area, and the river was compelled
to adjust accordingly. The river became seen as an engine for agricultural, urban, navigational, and –
later – industrial, development. Emblematic of many rivers in the modern era, a utilitarian mental-
ity dominated Trinity culture, focused on use of the river. Buckling under high expectations and
exploitations the river was doomed to disappoint: intermittent in the summer, heavily flooding in
spring and fall. It never became the navigation channel the city of Dallas had envisioned since its
founding in 1841. Serious levels of pollution in the early 20th century caused it to be called septic, 'the
Stench', the 'mythological river of death.' Its natural floods became such a big problem, especially in
the urbanizing areas of the Upper Trinity basin, that Dallas – in the largest engineering project of the
time – re-located the river out of the city's center, a move with significant negative consequences for
the Trinity's 'new neighbors', communities of color. It comes as no surprise that the Trinity occupied
an underdog place in the cultural imagination for many decades. This began to change with the rise
of the environmental movement in the United States in the 1970s and the major federal legislation
in its wake. The Trinity River is emblematic of many an American river, percolating into this new
era, into a new life, a new cultural imagination of growing awareness of environmental causes and
mounting concerns about pollution. Slowly the Trinity moved from being a burden into being an
asset, a new kind of asset. The virtually done-deal to make Dallas a port city by channelizing the
Trinity River all the way to the Gulf of Mexico into a straight 300-mile shipping canal – the old asset –
was defeated in a 1973 referendum, by invoking the new asset, the wealth of the riverine landscape
(Living with the Trinity 2010). Slowly but certainly, a major, new, cultural meander emerged, trea-
suring the Trinity, the Trinity River bottomlands, the hardwood forests, the prairies, the floods pro-
viding spawning sites for fish, the bird migration routes. The shift in mentality has been crucial for
biodiversity in the highly anthropogenic Trinity River, which is heavily leveed and impounded and
partially effluent-dominated during the summer months. We will illustrate this through the endemic
freshwater mussels and the native ancient Alligator Gar and Paddlefish. The cultural narrative arc
around the Alligator Gar, one of the largest freshwater fish, can be seen as symbolic of the Trinity
River's trajectory through time: from trash to trophy.

                                                    Trinity River

 Countries in the           United States of America
 catchment
 Catchment size (km2)       46,619
 Length (km)                1,150.6
 Discharge (m3 s-1)         Annual mean 630 (minimum 330, maximum 1,012) at the Liberty gage 1973–present
 Hydrological pattern       Discharge follows the bimodal rainfall pattern in the watershed with peak
                            amounts in both the late spring and the early fall, lowest water levels occur in July
                            and August in the Upper Trinity but earlier in the Lower Trinity.
 Degree of naturalness      The river is heavily modified with 31 reservoirs with capacities of more than
                            6 million m3. Additionally, there are more than 60 wastewater and other types
                            of effluent dischargers permitted to release 3,500 m3 d-1 or more, including two
                            wastewater treatment plants each of which releases more than 600,000 m3 d-1
 Natural landscape          Three types of prairies (grassland savannah), two types of densely forested
 types                      savannah systems, a coniferous forest, large bottomland hardwood forest, coastal
                            prairie/marsh at the Trinity-San Jacinto Estuary.
 Impact types               Most regions have been heavily modified by either urbanization or agriculture.
                            Bottomland hardwood forests have been impacted by changes in flood regimes
                            (primarily caused by 13 reservoirs), areas in the lower basin, such as the coastal prairie/
                            marsh, by oil and gas exploration and pipelines. The river is also heavily leveed with
                            a height of over 9 m for approximately 36 km between Fort Worth and Dallas.
 Largest cities             Dallas (1.34 million) and Fort Worth (909,585), which are part of the Dallas-Fort
 (inhabitants)              Worth Metroplex (7.5 million as of 2019).
 Urbanization               The Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex in the upper Trinity is the main urban area in
                            the watershed. In the 21st century it has been one of the fastest growing regions in
                            the USA, followed by the Houston metropolitan area, which lies just outside the
                            watershed but is dependent on water from the Trinity River. Projections suggest that
                            more than half of the Texan population will be dependent on the Trinity River by 2050.
 Protected areas            State Parks and three federally protected areas including the Lyndon B. Johnson
                            National Grasslands, the Trinity River National Wildlife Refuge, and the Menard
                            Creek Waterway Corridor of the Big Thicket National Preserve.
 Prevailing use form in     Major urban development in the upper Trinity. Intensive agricultural use includes
 the catchment              cattle and the cultivation of grains, hay and feed crops in the prairie landscapes,
                            fruit and vegetable crops in savannah forests, timber production in the coniferous
                            forests, and rice and pastures for cattle production in the coastal marsh areas.
                            Industrial use includes mostly oil and gas extraction and transport.
 Famous elements of         Alligator Gar (Atractosteus spatula), an iconic ancient fish species, and Trinity
 biodiversity               pigtoe (Fusconaia chunii), an endemic unionid mussel species.
 Famous elements of         Ancient Indigenous Clovis culture (13,000 BP). Caddo people, the Wichita, Kiowa,
 culture                    Comanche Hasinais, Anadarkos, Keechis, Ionis, Tawakonis and the Towash lived
                            in the basin. Spanish and French explorers pioneered the basin from 16th century
                            onwards. Early 19th century Anglo-American settler colonialism culture, a rural
                            culture of agricultural production, including slave-based cotton farming and a
                            cowboy ranching culture. Since early 20th century, the 'wildcatter' culture describes
                            hardworking, hard-playing oil extraction, entrepreneurial culture dominated
                            the metropolitan areas. Early 21st century, urban revitalization, recreation, and
                            environmental interests, led to new cultural engagement with the river and its
                            greenspaces. Fishing has always been an important cultural component.
