20 The Várzeas of the Brazilian Amazon River: Living with the
       Flood Pulse



Junk, Wolfgang J.1, Schöngart, Jochen2, Piedade, Maria T.F.2, Soares, Gercilia M.2,
Wittmann, Florian3

1
   National Institute for Science and Technology in Wetlands (INCT-INAU), Federal University of
    Mato Grosso, Cuiabá, Mato Grosso, Brazil
2
   National Institute for Amazon Research (INPA), Ecology, Monitoring and Sustainable Use of
   Wetlands (MAUA), Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil
3
   Institute of Wetland Ecology, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), Rastatt, Germany



                                                     Summary

The floodplains of the Amazon River and its whitewater tributaries, locally called várzeas, are
nutrient-rich and highly productive ecosystems. They have been colonized by humans for some
12,000 years. Today their main uses are agriculture, cattle and water buffalo ranching, extraction
of timber and other forest products, and fisheries. These activities vary according to a monomodal
flood pulse that leads to pronounced periods of drought and flooding during the annual cycle. Until
the end of the last century, the flood pulse was about 10 m in amplitude. During the last 30 years,
however, the annual amplitude has increased by 1.5 m on average, negatively affecting agriculture
and livestock production.
Large-scale agriculture is not possible, because of the heterogeneity of the highly dynamic river-
scape. Small family farms use the natural levees along the river and main channels, which allow boat
traffic throughout the year. Productivity per unit area is high for vegetables and production near
urban centers providing a considerable economic return. Such farming is labor-intensive and retains
many people in the várzeas. Cattle and buffalo ranching have led to deforestation of vast areas of
the várzeas to provide pastureland. Productivity per unit area is low on the ranches, which employ
relatively few people. Both ranchers and farmers are impacted by extreme floods and droughts.
Extraction of timber from floodplain forests is economically important, but highly selective and eco-
logically unsustainable causing declines in species diversity. Timber plantations require long-term
investment and their economic return remains untested in practice. Subsistence fishing provides
a vital source of protein for the rural population, whereas commercial fisheries supply the urban
centers.
Different approaches have been developed to assist politicians and planners to regulate the use of
várzea resources. The multiple-use approach advocates the balanced use of all várzea resources as
the most efficient form of management. Agronomic zonation provides information about the eco-
nomic potential of the different wetland uses, depending on their distance from markets, whereas
hydrologic zonation shows their level of vulnerability along the flooding gradient. Decentralized
participatory approaches to fisheries management, developed since the 1990s in the várzeas in the
vicinity of the city of Santarém, have brought to light the many practical and political problems in
the várzeas that must be addressed by a multiple-use approach. Wise political leadership is required
to regulate the activities of the different stakeholders, a responsibility that the Brazilian states and
national governments have yet to assume.

    ture – Life as a Dance to the Rhythm of the Waters. Pp. 469–495. UNESCO Publishing, Paris. DOI: 10.54677/

20.5.2 Agriculture
Várzea soils are among the most fertile in Cen-
tral Amazonia (Furch 2000), but their period-
ic inundation results in a short period suitable
for crop plantation during the low-water period
(fig. 20.2). Peak flooding in the central part of the
Amazon occurs around June. After the flood re-
cedes, the soil must be left to dry for a couple
of weeks before planting can start. During the
dry period, which extends from August to Oc-
tober, growing crops must be irrigated by motor
pumps, which is expensive and requires consis-
tent access to water. Nonetheless, subsistence           Fig. 20.5 Home garden. Photo: Jochen Schöngart

of several months duration, allow the successive

   Flood flows also serve to connect the function-
al network of the river system, from source to es-
tuary, spatially and over time. In addition to the
interconnection of the floodplain with the parent
river, there is an interconnection with the adja-
cent upland. This interconnection is easily de-
tectable by the periodic migration of terrestrial
animals to the uplands during rising water lev-
els, and their return to the dry floodplain during
the low-water period. Less conspicuous, but of
larger evolutionary importance, is the slow en-
trance of plants and animals from the uplands
into the floodplain over long periods of time,
which has led to the development of adaptations

                                                    Summary

The Pantanal is a huge, seasonal floodplain wetland in central South America. In the triangle of the
countries of Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay, the Upper Paraguay River floods an area of approxima-
tively 180,000 km² between December and June. The flood pulse migrates from the northern to the
southern part of the ca. 700 km long floodplain, and due to the expansion-contraction cycle, the peak
of the flood moves in a north-south direction over three months. Arid conditions and natural bush-
fires during the drought period concentrate the aquatic fauna in the remaining rivers, flood channels,
lakes and swamps. Humans, as well as fauna and flora, have developed remarkable adaptive traits to
cope with these extreme conditions. The original population of native indigenous peoples has been
strongly decimated. Some of their cultural elements are still alive, however, and have influenced
the 'Pantaneiro' culture of the traditional fishers and ranchers that have lived in the Pantanal over
several 100 years. This makes the Pantanal a showcase of how 'living in the rhythm of the waters' is
possible. In the past decades, however, economic interests have triggered enormous environmental
pressures. In the catchment of the Upper Paraguay River, a fast-growing number of dams disturbs
the natural flow regime and interrupts migration routes for the most important fish species. Industri-
al agriculture releases enormous amounts of eroded soils and pesticides, while fast-expanding cities

 from its catchment. Graph: André V. Nunes


with badly working sanitation systems pollute the rivers. Inside the Pantanal, modernization of cat-
tle ranching and crop agriculture homogenizes the highly diverse, park-like landscape, eliminates
the sustainable but less cost-efficient landuse forms, and erodes biocultural diversity. Policies favor-
ing fisheries tourism over traditional, artisanal fishing further contribute to a rural exodus. Climate
change and expansion of farmland have led to untimely and deleterious, man-made fires. The trans-
boundary Hidrovia project plans to transform the highly dynamic Paraguay River into a waterway
navigable for larger vessels, which would dramatically reduce living conditions for all wetland biota
and traditional cultures. Existing conservation and sustainable management plans urgently need to
be implemented. Cultural adaptations to the floodplain inundation cycle and techniques of common
resource sharing still exist and could serve as examples for other places.

   The Pantaneiro culture of traditional cattle
ranchers started to appear in the mid-18th century.
The first land was given to ranchers by the Por-
tuguese crown in 1727 (da Silva and Silva 1995)
and the first cattle ranches were established by
1737 (de Abreu et al. 2010) (fig. 21.6). Land titles,
however, were only ratified with the 1850 'Law of
Land' in an attempt to formalize the occupation
promoted during the 18th century (Silva and da
Silva 1995). Today, cattle ranchers and fishermen
are considered as Traditional Pantaneiro people,
recognized by the National Policy of Traditional
Peoples and Communities in the Brazilian law
number 6040 (Chiaravalloti 2019).

21.3.4 Modern times
Over the past decades, the Pantanal has reached
a crossroads (Junk and Nunes da Cunha 2005).
Many traditional settlers, both, Pantaneiros and
indigenous peoples, are still living as subsistence
smallholders (Junk and Nunes da Cunha 2005,
Wantzen et al. 2008b). In contrast, strong interests
in using the assets of the Pantanal for more lar-

                                                             The rhythm of rising and falling waters has char-
                                                             acterized human life in the Pantanal since its ear-

 Fig. 21.7 Wood storks (Mycteria americana) breed in large   resulted in cultural adaptations (River Culture,

The Pantanal: How long will there be Life in the Rhythm of the Waters?                                                 507


the indigenous peoples, the Guató have devel-
oped remarkable cultural features, including the
building of earth mounds and the displacement
in canoes (see early studies by Max Schmidt and
Branka Susnik, cited in current work by Eremites
de Oliveira (2000, 2003, 2011, 2017). Man-made
earth mounds can be found in different places
of the world, e.g. in the Mississippi delta (Gib-
son 2006, Whitney et al. 2013), and Australian
floodplains (Brockwell 2006). In the Pantanal,
they are spread all over the floodplain. Cultural
adaptations adopted by the traditional commu-
nities (Chiaravalloti et al. 2017, Tomas et al. 2019)
are better studied than those of the indigenous
groups, since most of these disappeared after
colonization.

22 Bio- and Cultural Diversity in The Middle Paraná River



Blettler, Martín1, Espínola, Luis A.1, Berros, Valeria2

1
     Instituto Nacional de Limnología (INALI; CONICET-UNL), Santa Fe, Argentina
2
     Centro de Investigaciones de la Facultad de Ciencias Jurídicas y Sociales, Universidad Nacional
      del Litoral (UNL), Santa Fe, Argentina



                                                     Summary

The Middle Paraná River (MPR) runs 722 km from the Paraguay-Paraná Rivers confluence to the city
of Diamante (Entre Ríos province, Argentina) and belongs to the La Plata Basin. The MPR has a large
floodplain of 6 to 40 km wide, with permanent and temporary water bodies (lakes, ponds, secondary
channels, tributaries and creeks) and the main channel shows a typical anabranching pattern (con-
strictions, sandy bars, islands, expansions) with mobile, sandy bed sediments.
The MPR-floodplain system is environmental and socially relevant since i) it is an important biolog-
ical corridor, ii) it is an important wetland that provides habitat and food for millions of individuals
from thousands of species (including endangered species), iii) it is an important route and stepping
stone for bird and fish migrations, iv) water and other natural resources such as fish are important
in the regional and subsistence economy, favoring artisanal fishing, ranching and tourism, and v) it
harbors a rich cultural diversity and is an important source of artistic and spiritual inspiration.
The seasonally alternating lifestyle with sedentary phases and short migratory movements has been
the main characteristic of all indigenous groups that inhabited the MPR. This feature is shared with
many native species of this large river system, suggesting a particular link between the riverine
societies and the river nature. However, today the entire Paraná River is threatened by different al-
terations and human impacts. The hydrological regime and biotic communities of this river section
have been experiencing considerable changes over the last 50 years as a consequence of the large
damming works established especially in the upper basin (Upper Paraná in Brazil), which has im-
pacted the lower reaches. In addition, the riparian vegetation is highly degraded and deforestation
in certain areas acquires alarming characteristics. A planned huge river work (the Paraguay-Paraná
waterway) would severely impact the natural hydromorphological dynamics. Other serious prob-
lems are the extreme plastic pollution as a direct consequence of the mismanagement of solid urban
waste, and the increasing cattle raising activities which promotes the fast degradation of this envi-
ronment.
On the other hand, much can be learned from the traditional ecological knowledge and the biotic
adaptations to the natural flow regime as elements of sustainable river management all over the
world.

                                                   Summary

The Rhine River can be considered as a connector between the Alpine Mountains and the Atlantic
Ocean. It is one of the most frequented waterways and one of the most important economic regions
in Europe. In spite of very old (15 My) sediments, most of its biocultural features developed after the
last glaciation, about 15,000 years ago. The Rhine is a classical example of environmental degradation
in the period after the Second World War, and a showcase of recovery since the 1990s, driven by in-
ternational collaborations, which may be used as an example for other strongly degraded rivers. Due
to the improved environmental quality, some biota have returned (e.g., beaver, salmon), the higher
water quality facilitates drinking water production, and the local population re-appreciates the clean
river for leisure activities. In terms of habitat quality much has yet to be done, though, especially con-
cerning the passability for migratory fish and restoration and reconnection of floodplain habitats. The
Rhine has become a crossroads for invasive species. Many of the traditional use forms such as salmon
and eel fisheries, wood rafting, ship mills, and towing of ships on the riverside have been abandoned,
as they were not possible anymore due to environmental pollution, or outdated. The outstanding
cultural landscape of the Middle Rhine has been inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage site in 2002.
The Rhine romanticism, a cultural movement cherishing the beauty of nature and architecture of the
Rhine in the 19th century, is used for touristic marketing today. The appreciation of the Rhine as a
cultural and socio-economic integrator in Europe, overcoming national disputes, engenders strong
social, cultural and economic activities and the development of transboundary institutions in the
Upper Rhine region such as EUCOR – The European Campus, the International Commission on the
Protection of the Rhine and the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine.

23.6 Current trends
23.6.1 Problem analysis
Depending on the point of view, the Rhine can
be considered both, a nightmare and a dream
for river ecologists: as a nightmare, as its biolog-
ical and cultural diversities have been so heavi-
ly degraded, and as a dream, as one of the most
polluted rivers has returned to life within such a
short time (Wantzen et al. 2021).

24 River Restoration on Catchment Scale in the Metropolitan Region
       and Post-Mining Landscape of the Emscher Catchment, Germany



Gerner, Nadine V.1, Sommerhäuser, Mario M.1, Heldt, Sonja1, Sutcliffe, Robynne1, Stein, Ulf2,
Tröltzsch, Jenny2

1
   Department River and Landscape, Emschergenossenschaft/Lippeverband (EGLV), Essen,
    Germany
2
   Ecologic Institut gemeinnützige GmbH, Berlin, Germany



                                                       Summary

The Emscher River Catchment in the federal state of North-Rhine Westphalia, Germany, has ex-
perienced a century of intensive mining, steel industry expansion, and population growth, during
which time the entire river network was transformed into an open wastewater drain, straightened
and with concrete beds and dikes. Such an open infrastructure system was the only solution given
the risk of ground subsidence due to underground coal mining. Now mining has ended, the man-
made open wastewater system is being restored as far as possible towards near-natural streams. The
restoration on catchment scale is a 30-year endeavor with costs summing up to more than € 5 billion.
Soon after restoration, the upper river course and the tributary streams already exhibited more nat-
ural features, but the re-establishment of a diverse aquatic community is expected to take at least ten
years. The Emscher River and its restored tributaries now provide places for recreation, which are
in high demand in this most densely populated area of Germany. The people in the region are now
rediscovering the Emscher River after they had learned to avoid the former open sewers throughout
an entire century. Participatory projects invite people to learn about the returning biodiversity and
to get active in monitoring the development of the streams as citizen scientists. The restoration of the
streams also acts as a trigger for a structural change in the entire region, leading to a higher attrac-
tiveness of cities, and thus, to a better quality of life. Overall, a wide range of ecosystem services is
again provided by the riverscape. However, new challenges have to be tackled, including the arrival
of invasive non-native species in the freshly restored aquatic habitats, as well as the more extreme
rainfall and drought events as part of climate change.

separation of urban wastewater from the higher

ued at more than € 5 billion, the Emscher's resto-
ration or 'Emscher re-conversion' began, also con-
ducted by the Emschergenossenschaft (fig. 24.2).
It is regarded as one of the world's biggest socio-
ecological restoration projects. As part of the res-
toration, four large wastewater treatment plants
and 400 km of sewers were built, allocating the
wastewater underground. Above ground, the
350 km of now wastewater-free open sewers were
restored to 'near-natural' streams, starting with
the tributaries and the upper section of the Em-
scher River before restoring the Emscher main-
stem (Emschergenossenschaft 2015).

in the region no longer avoid the river, but in-
stead are starting to rediscover its River Culture
(Wantzen et al. 2016). As the region is so dense-
ly urbanized, there is a high demand for natural
surroundings and places for recreation. The riv-

24.5.2 The discovery of the Emscher River
        System for recreation
Not only the IBA, but also the start of the Emscher
River restoration triggered structural change
in the wider region. The Emscher and its tribu-
taries are linear corridors that connect 16 cities.
As restored blue-green elements, they enhance
the aesthetic value of landscapes and of cities,
making them more attractive for people and
companies. Prominent examples are Lake Phoe-
nix in Dortmund, Zollverein Coal Mine Indus-
trial Complex (Zeche Zollverein) in Essen, and
Duisburg Nord Landscape Park (fig. 24.10), as
described below.
                                                       Fig. 24.10a Lake Phoenix in Dortmund. Photo: Markus
   Lake Phoenix is an artificial lake located di-      Greulich, Emschergenossenschaft, with permission
rectly next to the restored Upper Emscher. The
lake was constructed on the site of a former steel
plant demolished in 2001. A comprehensive feasi-
bility study was conducted, coordinated by Em-
schergenossenschaft and the City of Dortmund,
before this extraordinary idea was turned into
reality. As several objectives could be achieved
under a common vision, all the involved actors
fully supported the endeavor. The lake serves as a
flood retention basin and offers enormous ecolog-
ical, economic, and social values. A species-rich
and resilient ecosystem has developed in and
around the lake. In a 24-hour biodiversity count
more than 500 species were detected in the water
and along the shore (GEO day of biodiversity in
                                                       Fig. 24.10b Zollverein Coal Mine Industrial Complex in
2015). The lake is now one of the most important
                                                       Essen. Photo: Martin Baier, Emschergenossenschaft, with
habitats for resident and migrating birds in the
                                                       permission
catchment (Kretzschmar et al. 2020). At the same
time, the lakeside is the most popular new hous-
ing area in Dortmund. Regarding recreation, the
lake and riverscape offer new opportunities for
sports (running, cycling, and sailing), as well as
walking, relaxation and nature observation.
   Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord also used
to be a steel production plant. It was closed in
1985 and transformed into a recreational and
event park, but without the plant being demol-
ished. The old buildings now house various
events and contain, among many others, a dive
tank, youth hostel, and restaurant. Bike paths, a
climbing area, and a garden are located on the
site as well. The location is very popular, receiv-

25 The Isar River: Social Pride as a Driver of River Restoration



Zingraff-Hamed, Aude1, 2, Lupp, Gerd1, Bäumler, Klaus3, Huang, Joshua1, Pauleit, Stephan1

1
   Chair for Strategic Landscape Planning and Management, Technical University of Munich,
    Freising, Germany
2
   CNRS UMR 7324 CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, France
3
   Münchner Forum. Diskussionsforum für Entwicklungsfragen e.V., Munich, Germany



                                                    Summary

The transboundary Isar River is an alpine river that flows through the Bavarian Alps to join the
Danube River in one of its last free-flowing sections. The Isar enables local human development and
crosses the city of Munich that is the 12th largest city in Europe. The Isar largely contributes to the
successful growth of Munich and highly influences the cultural development of other cities built on
or close to its floodplain. The alpine riverscape is highly appreciated by the local population and is
a source of civic pride. The socio-ecological degradation of the Isar River started in the late 18th cen-
tury with the first morphological changes. However, it is the boom in hydro-electrical production
after the First World War that caused the greatest river degradations. Because of the clear response
from civil society, advocacy groups pushed for the restoration of the river. After many years of
collaborative planning, intense discussion, pressure from civil society, changes in government in-
stitutions, and strong partnerships among non-government organizations, the river management
trend changed from a traditional grey infrastructure-based to nature-based practices. The Isar-Plan,
namely the Isar restoration project in Munich was very successful and became a worldwide symbol
of hope, showing that socio-ecological restorations are possible even in metropolitan city centers.
Ultimately, the Isar River is an example showing how civil society's perception of ecosystem losses
can positively influence water governance.

       of a Great European River

"In treating [the river] as a machine we have literally and conceptually disassembled the river. It has become to
its users a set of separate spaces and parts. Fishermen see habitat. Irrigators see water. Power managers, utility
operators, and those who run aluminium factories see reservoirs necessary to turn turbines. Barge owners see
channels with certain depths of water. Environmentalists see brief stretches of free-flowing water. All stake a
social claim to their part of the machine. None of them are concerned with the river as a whole."
                                                                                                     White 1995, p. 110



                                                      Summary

The Danube is the second largest river of Europe, it drains the most international river basin on earth
shared by 19 countries. The Danube is the only major river connecting central and eastern regions in
Europe and as an important migration corridor for organisms, the Danube connects regions adjacent
to its basin in the west and east. Due to this geographic orientation and a high number of ecoregions,
the Danube River Basin, and the Danube Delta in particular, are regions of exceptional high freshwa-
ter biodiversity. The Danube's hydromorphological features differ significantly between the upper,
middle, and lower sections and in the Delta. The river has been an important border zone as well as
a route for transport and migration since the earliest phases of human history of the Danube. The
fossil-fuel-based process of industrialization significantly changed the riverine landscapes and the
drivers of this environmental transformation. Starting in the late 18th century mainly at the Upper
Danube, industrialization gradually seized the entire basin and dramatically accelerated after World
War II, during the 'Cold War' on both sides of the 'Iron Curtain'. Land reclamation and flood protec-
tion for urban agglomerations, waterborne heavy transport and hydropower became the dominant
forms of (over)exploiting the river in modern times. Today, main pressures impacting the ecological
integrity of these industrialized riverine landscapes include the fragmentation by dams especially in
the Upper Danube, the poor water quality in the middle and lower Danube sections, and the high
number of invasive species threatening aquatic biodiversity as well as the loss of floodplain areas
in all river sections. The International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River Basin
(­ICPDR) is responsible for the transboundary water management ensuring the sustainable and equi-
table use of waters in the Danube River Basin.

1785–1788). Because transport costs were high
and staple food was therefore traded from out-
side only in exceptional cases, alluvial sites were
sometimes also used for grain cultivation. The
spatial distribution of different land use types
in the Danube floodplains in Machland was well
adapted to environmental conditions. Meadows
and pastures were located in the most dynamic
zones along the two main Danube arms, which
existed prior to channelization (Hohensinner
et al. 2004). If these areas were eroded, the loss
was less harmful than in arable land. If fields,
but also orchards, buildings and roads had to be
established in the floodplains, they were located
in zones, which were inundated but not washed
away. In addition, the highest elevations were
chosen. Of course, also in the 19th century, floods
were predominantly seen as negative. Neverthe-
less, pre-industrial societies depending solely on
natural fertilizers also saw the positive effects
of river floods: the Danube water brought in
nutrients that fostered plant growth (e.g., Zech-
meister 1846). When river channelization started
in several sections of the Upper Danube in the
middle of the 19th century (see table 26.2), for-
estry management plans regularly mourned the
negative effects of this loss of fertilization due to
interrupted inundation (Finsterer 2000).
   While the Machland demonstrates how people
in a rural area dealt with the Danube's flood risk,
the situation was different in urban areas. Since
the middle ages, Vienna and Budapest evolved
as important urban centers of the later Habsburg
Empire, both cities exhibited fast growth during
the 19th century. In contrast to other European

27 The Seine, the River dedicated to Paris



Lestel, Laurence1, Meybeck, Michel1, Carré, Catherine2, Belliard, Jérôme3

1
   UMR 7619 METIS, Sorbonne Université-CNRS-EPHE, Paris, France
2
   LADYSS, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, Paris, France

   HYCAR Research Unit, INRAE, Antony, France



                                                    Summary

In France, the Seine River was already being used as a waterway some 6000 years ago. It has favored
the development of Paris since the Romans founded the city as Lutetia. In the Middle Ages, the
transportation of timber rafts and food supplies on the river, river mills, and direct use of the water
supply sustained the growth of the capital city. New river uses were developed in the mid-19th centu-
ry: the river was gradually channelized and equipped with locks for navigation and received insuffi-
ciently treated urban wastewater. During the same period, the Seine riverscape was immortalized by
impressionist painters. From 1870 to 1970, the river quality downstream of Paris continued to wors-
en in a context of urban development: few fish species survived, due to severe hypoxia in the Lower
Seine, until a giant wastewater treatment plant, Seine-Aval, was constructed in the 1940s–1990s.
This effort led to an improved basic environmental quality in the 1990s, which allowed the gradual
restoration of fish populations downstream of Paris. The longitudinal and transversal connectivity
of the river was again reduced after World War II: major reservoirs were built in the headwaters for
flood control and sustaining low flows in the river reach within Paris, and the original floodplain
wetlands were transformed into several hundred artificial sand pits. Today, migratory fishes are
now gradually returning, including salmon in the lower part of the river, thanks to specific fishways
which partially restore migration pathways.
From 1960 to 2010, Parisians had very little contact with their river: fluvial navigation, flood control,
sand extraction, river bank car traffic, and poor water quality were the limiting factors. The inscrip-
tion of the banks of the Seine in Paris by UNESCO on the World Heritage list in 1991, signaled a
reversed trend in the expectations of the riverside residents concerning their river. Associations and
officials have since requested the ecological restoration of urban rivers, including the Seine, and
the conservation of the few remaining natural wetlands. Recreational amenities were re-established
from the 2000s onwards, and the swimming competitions, planned for the Paris Olympic Games in
2024, are a driver to reach a better bacteriological river quality. However, the Seine River, impacted
by a metropole of seven million people and its related impacts, is set to remain a highly modified
river, and will continue to be regulated to provide the economic functionalities and restored to pro-
vide the ecological functionalities expected today; coordinated governance at the scale of the whole
river basin, successful in terms of water quality, has yet to be realized in other domains such as flood
security or habitat restoration.

                                                  Summary

The valley of the Loire River combines rich cultural with biological diversity. Benefitting from a
mild climate, fertile soils and a rich fish fauna, it has attracted human settlers since its early days, but
its inundations have also been feared. It is a biogeographical and cultural corridor connecting the
French Central Massif mountains to the Atlantic coast, in which alternating Celtic (Gaul), Roman,
and Christian-Western cultural elements have coalesced to a unique and exceptional value honored
as a World Heritage Site by the UNESCO. Despite being most famous for wine and chateaux, the
Loire can also serve as an example for sustainable environmental management by applying a ba-
sin-wide management plan. Social movements in the 1980s have helped to preserve the largest part
of the river from damming. However, damming of headwaters, lateral diking and excessive sand
extraction have caused a severe (avg. 1.5 m) incision of the river bed and decreasing hydromorpho-
logical dynamics, resulting in shrinking floodplain habitats, and, recently, a fixation of large parts
of the alluvium by trees. Projects to remobilize sediments by dike and groyne removal are going on,
however, the release of sediments from headwaters has not yet been taken into consideration. Cur-
rently, climate change heats the water and the debates about water use in this unique river.

 are shaped by the river. Many buildings have been constructed using the limestone from the escarpments. The caves

                                                  Summary

Connecting the volcanic mountains of the Massif Central to the Atlantic Ocean, the Dordogne River
has long been and is still the backbone for the local development of human and non-human life. The
480 km-long river provides numerous habitats for fauna and flora and constitutes a migratory route
for fish and birds. Despite the presence of one of the three France's largest chains of dams, the Dor-
dogne basin is still a refuge for rare European species such as the eight major diadromous migrating
fish, the European otter, the European mink, or the freshwater pearl mussel. The Dordogne river
and its valley have played a major role in human development over the centuries, even since early
times, and offer a huge diversity of landscapes and architectural remains. Prehistoric caves, medie-
val castles and villages, old mills stand alongside hydropower dams dating from the late 19th century
and Art Deco style buildings. Even though the relation between humans and the river has changed
over the years, the Dordogne is still deeply rooted in the local culture and economy, either with the
use of water as a power and as a resource for fishing or as an attractive asset for leisure and tourist
activities. The legends and the old stories linked to the river are fertile grounds for local celebra-
tions and represent an interesting medium to raise people's awareness about environmental issues.
The long-lasting attempts of the local communities to develop while preserving the rivers and their
resources have been internationally recognized when the Dordogne basin has entered the list of
UNESCO Biosphere Reserves as the first one in the world to cover an entire watershed. This designa-
tion has encouraged local public authorities, researchers, and communities to carry out studies and
experimentations with the aim of mitigating the progressive loss of biodiversity and anticipating the
negative effects of climate change on human and non-human populations.

       Delta (Spain)



Mariano, Mercè1, Abella, Susanna2, Araujo, Rafael3, Ibisate, Askoa4, Ollero, Alfredo5

1
   Terres de l'Ebre Environmental Policies Consortium, Amposta, Spain
2
   Platform in Defence of the Ebro (PDE), Tortosa, Spain
3
   Natural Sciences National Museum-CSIC, Madrid, Spain (in memoriam)
4
   Department of Geography, Prehistory and Archaeology, University of the Basque Country,
    UPV/EHU, Vitoria-Gasteiz, Spain

   Department of Geography and Territorial Planning, University of Zaragoza, Zaragoza, Spain


                                                     Summary

The Ebro is one of the largest river basins in Southern Europe, with an area of 85,000 km2, a river length
of 930 km, and a population of more than three million people. Since ancient times, it has not only been a
resource, but also a channel for communication, commerce and the settlement of great civilizations along
its course. The Ebro Basin has always been rich in cultural heritage and blessed with a diverse biology. It
hosts a wide variety of endemic species, some of which are now endangered by human-induced threats.
Spain is one of the most vulnerable countries in Europe concerning climate change. It also has a long
history of human-water relationships, evident from Roman (after 197 BC) and Umayyad-Muslim
(after 711 AD) influences; both cultures are famous for their water management technologies. The
Ebro River waters, coming from the Pyrenees mountain range with which it flows almost in parallel
southwards, have always been coveted. Over the centuries, land and water exploitation have pro-
gressively intensified, and the most recent transformations have resulted in the Ebro now being one
of the most stressed rivers in the world.
A great number of large reservoirs produce a big amount of energy but have significantly changed
the river's flow and sediment regimes. This regulation, combined with excessive water extraction for
irrigation and drinking water in its thirsty surroundings, has been detrimental to almost all aspects
of the river ecosystem. The highest impact is visible at the delta, which suffers from compaction, sub-
sidence, and regression, today receiving less than 5% of the river's original sediment load. Despite
being administered by one of the oldest hydrographic management organizations worldwide, the
increasing overall water locations and subsequent environmental and social problems in the Ebro
Basin area are a source of considerable on-going conflict and debate. This situation has given rise to
one of the most powerful social movements in defense of the Ebro River.
Several initiatives are underway to reverse the detrimental losses of natural geodiversity and function-
ality, by maintaining flows that sustain ecological health, giving natural space back to the river and im-
proving human flood defense systems. Nevertheless, much remains to be done, and ongoing challenges
can only be effectively tackled through well-directed (and previously-lacking) institutional will, backed
by broad public consensus. If not, what has taken countless centuries to create will be lost in less than one.

 Degree of naturalness        There are contradictory published statements about the degree of naturalness:
                              – Official statements (CHE 2018) indicate that 16% of the waterbodies are highly
                                 modified, and that 31% of natural areas have no proposals to achieve good
                                 ecological status.
                              – According to a revision of the river basin management plans by the European
                                 Commission (EC 2019), however 19% of the Ebro River is highly modified. If
                                 implemented, new management plans (CHE 2018) will increase the area under
                                 irrigation, further reducing flows (and connectivity to the floodplain), and
                                 increasing pollution.
                              – About 25% of the delta is in a natural state, 65% is agricultural, and 10%
                                 urbanized.

 Type of natural              The Middle Ebro River is meandering, with a broad valley bottom and extensive
 landscape                    floodplain. The predominant land use is agriculture.
                              The Ebro Delta is a great plain, with some levees along the river banks. Reduced
                              sediment supplies (dams upstream) have caused delta shrinking and marine
                              transgressions. Predominant land use is salt-tolerant rice cultivation.

 Impact types                 The Ebro Basin has 125 dams of more than 1 hm3 with a total reservoir capacity of
                              8,000 hm3, regulating 60% of discharge and retaining 95% of sediments.
                              The main issue related to the basin pollution is the diffuse contamination caused
                              by intensive livestock and irrigation, which presents an almost irreversible
                              character. There is also a problem with pesticides in the Gallego basin. Both
                              animal and plant invasive species are abundant.
                              Middle Ebro: Longitudinal dykes and breakwaters further alter natural channel
                              dynamics and riparian forests.
                              Delta: The greatest current impact is the reduction of sediments due to dams

                              The main urbanization process occurred between 1960 and 1990 with a significant

 Predominant river            Agricultural food production, with cereal and forage crops supporting more
 basin land use               than 30% of Spain's commercial meat production. The starch and sweetener

                              Delta: rice growing, fishing and fish farming predominate
 Renowned                     Middle Ebro River: Important habitats include the meandering main channel,
 biodiversity elements        riparian forests and galachos (oxbows, ancient meanders), and tertiary
                              escarpment. Unionid mussel species in danger of extinction, such as Pseudunio
                              auricularius (syn. Margaritifera auricularia) and Unio mancus, and fish species (e.g.,
                              Salaria fluviatilis, Parachondrostoma miegii, Luciobarbus graellsii).
                              Delta: habitats of great environmental importance/value, such as bays, coastal
                              oxbow lakes, river network, the Ebro Sea, the Fangar and Alfacs bays, coastal
                              sandbars and dune beaches, ullals (freshwater upwellings), and salt flats. The
                              enormous variety of aquatic habitats favors the coexistence of marine and
                              freshwater species. 337 of the almost 600 bird species in Europe have been
                              registered, notably > 60% of the world population of Audouin's gull, Larus
                              audouinii. Among plants, e.g., Limonastrium monopetalum and Zygopuillum album
                              are noteworthy.
 Renowned cultural            Navigation along the Middle Ebro, with downriver wood transportation until
 elements                     the 1950s. The Imperial Canal (in Aragón) is a symbol of this stretch of the Ebro .
                              In the Lower Ebro, traditional techniques such as making traditional fishing nets
                              and construction of huts using reeds and mud, existed from the Middle Ages to
                              the 20th century. In the Middle and Lower Ebro, the folkloric jota dance, of Arabic
                              origin, spread upstream due to river trade.
                              In the delta, characteristic elements are the hut architecture, rice culture, and the
                              emblematic metallic Buda lighthouse (built in 1864), a mobile lighthouse that
                              could be dismantled and re-erected. Since 2000, there is a strong social movement
                              aimed at defense of the Ebro River and regaining a river identity (Platform in
                              Defence of the Ebro).

   Alfacs and Fangar arrowhead sandbar and dune
beaches: Extensive sandy beaches and the largest
dune landscape in Catalonia are found within
the delta (fig. 30.7). Near the sea, the dunes are
mobile, while further inland they are more sta-
ble and partially vegetated with psammophilic
(moving sand-tolerant) species (e.g., beach tares,
burs and sea lilies). These species are adapt-
ed to the harsh living conditions, such as high
permeability of the soil and a high solar radia-
tion index 30. Behind these dunes, there exists
a splendid plant community with flowers of

(Psammodromus algirus). The beaches and dunes
are also breeding and resting sites for terns,
seagulls and waders. Even the endangered ma-

here.

   Miravet Castle and Xerta Weir: An example is
the medieval Castle of Miravet (fig. 30.12), an
exemplar of the architecture of the Order of the
Templars in Europe. Another built infrastruc-
ture for the use of the water resources of the
Ebro River and a testament to the Catalan indus-
trial heritage of the Renaissance is the Xerta Weir
(fig. 30.13), linked to which is also a disused flour
factory and mill. The weir is a 310 m diagonal
semi-circular weir/partial diversion where the
water flows evenly over the crest. It is believed
to have been built in Islamic times and restored
in the 12th century, but the works did not finish
until 1411. Later, in the 19th century, it was recon-   Fig. 30.13 Xerta weir. Photo: EliziR, Wikimedia Com-
                                                        mons, CC BY-SA 3.0
ditioned to redirect the water to the Ebro Right
and Left Bank Canals for rice irrigation.
   Navigation and boat crossings: Concerning the
navigability of the Lower Ebro, has given rise to
a rich heritage in terms of traditional boats and
boat crossings, as well as lost arts and crafts,
such as boatmen and towmen. In recent decades,
efforts were made to promote river tourism and
increase navigation and recover the popular cul-
ture and old trades with festive events. (i.e. River
festival in Flix with traditional punt boat races,
or to recover old techniques: rice planting or
harvesting festivals in various towns of the Del-
ta). Among the non-material cultural elements
related to river navigation, the boatman's trade        Fig. 30.14 Amposta suspension bridge. Photo: Mariano
is worth mentioning, dating back to the 12th cen-       Cebolla, with permission
tury. For centuries, the only crossing place in
the estuary final stretch of the Ebro Delta was
the Paso de las barcas (the boat crossing) in Tor-
tosa. The construction of the first bridges con-
demned the ferries to their disappearance (more
than 300 boat crossings were counted along the
Ebro River). In 2020, only three ferries remain:
in Miravet and Flix, and one recently restored,
in Garcia.
   Traditional punt boats: The Lower Ebro be-
tween Ascó and Amposta is now navigable and
recreational activities using traditional punt
boats, such as the llagut (Catalan), muleta or pon-
tona have been restored. The recovery of the rec-
reational and sports use of the Ebro continues its
history of the transportation of goods and peo-
ple that was common until the 1970s.
   As already mentioned in the history section,
the Ebro Delta was uninhabited until the middle
of the 19th century. With the construction of irri-
gation canals and land reclamation for rice culti-
vation, the first settlers came from the neighbor-
ing areas of Amposta and Tortosa, their cultural
features being common to the rest of the Ebro
Basin.

   Amposta suspension bridge and Lo passador
bridge: Following the course of the lower stretch
of the Ebro River and entering the estuary, we
come across viaducts and bridges built from 1868
onwards, among them the Amposta suspension
bridge (1915, the second bridge of this type in         Fig. 30.16 Typical delta barn or ''barraca del delta''.
the world, fig. 30.14) and the Sant Jaume d'Enve-       Photo: Mercè Mariano
ja bridge (2010). This design was chosen due to
the depth of the river channel and lack of stability
of the land. The bridge notably improved the ex-
change between the towns of the Ebro Delta, since
it was the first permanent crossing point within
the delta from 25 km to its mouth. It was only in
2010 that the "Lo Pasador" road bridge further
downstream connected the cities of Sant Jaume
d'Enveja and Deltebre, previously only connected
by barges (motorized since 1859). Lo Pasador ('the
ferry man') is the most significant modern archi-
tectural element in the delta and, at 12 m high, it
is one of its highest topographic points.

   Buda lighthouse: Among the most unique ar-           Cebolla, with permission
chitectural elements of the Ebro Delta are the
Buda Lighthouse (1864, fig. 30.15). Today, it lies
at the bottom of the Ebro Sea, more than 3 km off
the coast, and represents one of the main testi-
monies of the delta's recent regression.
   When the Buda Lighthouse was built as one of
the first lighthouses on the delta coast the Ebro
River still contributed so much sediment that the
delta and adjoining coast were rapidly advanc-
ing . Therefore, a metallic lighthouse was built
that could be dismantled and moved as the del-
ta grew. The Buda Lighthouse was active until
Christmas Day 1961, when it collapsed during

30.7.2 Recover natural flow dynamics of the
         Ebro River system
New social pressure has induced a reflection on
how to achieve sustainable development that
improves the quality and diversity of agricultur-
al products, without further water abstraction
or damage to the environment. In the case of the
Ebro, this would mean rethinking the manage-
ment of dams and water abstraction/irrigation
schemes, to recover, as far as possible, the con-
nectivity of the river and its natural ecohydro-
logical and morphological dynamics.

31 The Waterways of Venice as an 'Extended Museum':
       New Opportunities for Cultural, Social and Environmental
       Regeneration of a Forgotten Water Heritage



Eulisse, Eriberto1, Vallerani, Francesco2, Visentin, Francesco3

1
   Global Network of Water Museums and Civiltà dell'Acqua International Centre, Ca' Foscari
    University of Venice, Venice, Italy
2
   Department of Economics, Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Venice, Italy
3
   Department of Languages and Literature, Communication, Education, and Society, University of
    Udine, Udine, Italy



                                                     Summary

The evolution of the historical waterways of Venice, Italy, is considered from a transdisciplinary and
holistic perspective to analyze and redeem the legacy of forgotten waterscapes and related heritage.
Such a cultural and natural legacy reveals some remarkable examples of the Palladian landscape
built along inland waterways, rivers, and a fascinating network of channels as 'liquid roads'. The
river system dealt with here are watercourses that today flow into the Venice Lagoon (including the
Piave, Sile, Zero, Dese, Marzenego, Brenta, Bacchiglione, and Adige rivers), but also the mighty Po
River and its tributaries. When investigating the historical linkages between the hydraulic heritage
and natural environments, biocultural aspects and aquatic ecosystems appear as an unbreakable
unity – in spite of the different approaches to analyze them.
The heritage related to Venice's inland waterways will be also explored through the perspective of
a 'digital and extended museum' to stimulate multiple plans for a local re-evaluation of water assets
and a new ground-breaking holistic vision. Indeed, water museums (both physical and digital mu-
seums, as well as eco-museums and institutions that manage built infrastructures and architectures
strongly related to water) are key players to bridge past and present water knowledge, educate peo-
ple, and promote a new culture for sustainable living. This perspective today is formally endorsed
by the Resolution XXIII–5 of UNESCO's Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme (IHP 2018)
that aims at improving water awareness education in the frame of Agenda 2030 involving, in partic-
ular, water museums.
The perspective outlined here influenced the recognition of the above-mentioned resolution to cre-
ate a global partnership of water museums aimed at re-evaluating and rejuvenating inherited water
legacies worldwide. The approach designed to foster sustainable eco-tourism along Venice's inland
waterways shows how similar projects aiming to reconnect people to water can be promoted any-
where. Lessons learned from past generations through trial and error approaches in dealing locally
with water heritage are today more precious than ever, to educate for sustainable water manage-
ment in a rapidly changing world and find new solutions that benefit both people and nature.

   Rich and consistent water heritage can be
identified along the Venetian waterways – a
legacy made of hydraulic artefacts, small river
ports, riverbanks, and bridges, as well as elegant
riverside villas, traditional wooden boats and
small shipyards. Know-how and craftsmanship
to manage and deal with waterways were trans-
mitted through generations and are part of a pe-
culiar intangible heritage. Both this knowledge
and material assets layered the identity of all wa-
tercourses which have been strongly influenced
by Venice's culture and architecture for at least
five centuries.

The Waterways of Venice as an 'Extended Museum'                                                              789


 Table 31.1 Historical evolution of inland waterways in the Veneto region, Italy

       Phase                                                      Main events

 The Middle Ages         The origins of Venice's inland waterways that connect the river system with the
                         lagoon can be traced back to the 11th century AD, when the first hydraulic works
                         aimed at connecting the natural river system by means of artificial canals were made
                         to improve the transportation of goods, people, and the military. Waterways were
                         made functional to strengthen mobility and commerce, as the road system linking
                         inland towns to the coastal city of Venice and the flourishing Mediterranean trade was
                         poor.
 The Palladian           During the Renaissance (15–16th centuries), the development of the Venice system
 landscape               of inland waterways thrived most, thanks to new hydraulic techniques which were
                         functional to manage all river flows, including both small water courses that flow into
                         the lagoon and the Po River. Palladio's architectures and Canaletto's paintings record
                         and celebrate the aesthetic values of well-managed fluvial waters. The Palladian
                         landscape and related waterscapes marked the blossoming age of navigable inland
                         waterways.
 Transition              After the fall of the Republic of Venice (1797), the waterways system was no longer
                         regularly managed. However, during the Italian Kingdom (1861–1946) it was still
                         used, and often maintained, for river transport and military purposes. During World
                         War I, the inland waterways became a crucial asset for strategic military operations
                         aimed at defending Venice and its lagoon from Austro-Hungarian attacks.
 Degradation             After World War II, and especially from the 1960s onwards, the lack of adequate
                         public policies marked the inevitable abandonment of river trade. The loss of material
                         culture and craftsmanship was paralleled by the decline in local know-how and
                         intangible heritage. This decay generated the social loss of a 'fluvial sense of place'
                         and a disruption of ancestral perceptions and attitudes towards rivers and inland
                         waterscapes.
 The contemporary        In the last decade to the present day, there have been occasional attempts to
 setting for             reconsider historical waterways and rivers as 'blue corridors' for leisure activities,
 regeneration and        social recreation, and recovery of the hydraulic legacy. The research and project
 eco-tourism             perspective outlined here aims at promoting both the value of all hydraulic structures
                         and assets built along historical waterways and the revitalization of the related
                         aquatic ecosystems.

The research to build the 'digital and extend-
ed' Water Museum of Venice also generated an
unexpected outcome beyond the local scale. At
last, methods used to classify water assets, pro-
mote heritage access and sustainable mobility,
foster public participation, and frame several
new routes as a texture to implement a digital
and extended museum, provided a reference
model for building a network of water museums
and heritage sites on a global scale: the Global
Network of Water Museums (https://www.­
watermuseums.net/).

32 Ecohydrology and River Culture: Synergies for the Enhancement
       of River and Catchment Sustainability



Zalewski, Maciej1, 2, Wantzen, Karl M.3

1
  European Regional Centre for Ecohydrology PAS u/a UNESCO, Lodz, Poland
2
  UNESCO Chair Ecohydrology and Applied Ecology, University of Lodz, Lodz, Poland
3
  UNESCO Chair River Culture, CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, and CNRS
   UMR LIVE, University of Strasbourg, Strasbourg, France



                                                  Summary

The new challenges now facing environmental science demand a holistic approach that inte-
grates knowledge and translates it into innovations and systemic solutions, entailing a shift to
a new, evolutionary-ecosystemic paradigm. In this paper, we present the main tenets of Ecohy-
drology (Zalewski et al. 1997, Zalewski 2020) proposing catchment-wide ecohydrological river
management measures by integrating ecological and hydrological processes for enhancement of
its sustainability potential WBSRCE, and compare it to the River Culture Concept (Wantzen et
al. 2016). We conclude that the River Culture and Ecohydrology approaches share many com-
monalities and, if combined, the two approaches offer a promising framework for harnessing
greater societal involvement on behalf of river basin sustainability. In closing, we suggest a set of
four steps for accelerating this process of modifying attitudes and precipitating paradigm shift
from sociocentric-mechanistic to evolutionary-ecosystemic approaches for sustainable river basin
management.

33 Damming and Sediment Legacies of Great Rivers: Global
       Challenges and Management Approaches



Kondolf, G. Matt1, Schmitt, Rafael J.P.1, 2

1
  Riverlab, Department of Landscape Architecture and Environmental Planning, University of
   California, Berkeley, California, USA
2
  The Natural Capital Project, Stanford University, Stanford, California, USA



                                                  Summary

The sediment load of rivers is critically important to maintain the geometry of river channels and
coastal features that depend on the river-supplied sediment, such as beaches and deltas. Sediment
and nutrient transport in rivers is also crucial to support riverine and coastal fisheries and other eco-
systems supporting livelihoods and socio-cultural and economic practices. Human activities modify
sediment supply and transport, altering the sediment budgets of river basins. Sediment trapping by
dams and extraction of sand and gravel from river channels both interrupt the longitudinal conti-
nuity of sediment transport in the river and create sediment-starved, 'hungry water' downstream.
Either extreme increases or decreases in sediment supply can result in effects persisting for decades
or centuries as sediment legacies. The magnitude of the sediment starvation now being created by
the global proliferation of dams is unprecedented, and its legacy will be long-lasting. On the Me-
kong River, the riverine fishery that formerly supported 60 million people is now collapsing, largely
attributable to dams blocking migratory routes, cutting off natural sediment and nutrient loads,
and reducing seasonal water-level fluctuations needed to inundate large areas of floodplain for fish
habitat. The Mekong Delta is now losing land due to reduced sediment supply and accelerated
subsidence. Without urgent, substantive changes in management, most of this critically important
landscape feature will be lost by 2100.
To restore sediment continuity, sediments can be bypassed around dams and passed through dams
(techniques that are viable for many reservoirs, yet rarely implemented). Even better, in basins where
dams are still being planned and built, strategic planning tools can be used to select dam portfolios
that result in lower impacts to sediment continuity and sediment-related livelihoods, while still pro-
viding a sufficient amount of hydroelectric power, augmented by less-costly alternative renewable
energy, such as photovoltaic solar.

 Fig. 33.6 Power generation and sediment trapping from dam building in the Sre Pok, Se San, and Se Kong rivers (collec-
 tively known as the '3S basin'), the largest downstream tributary system to the Mekong River (drainage area 80,000 km2).
 (a) The current 3S dam portfolio includes 21 dams built or under construction, and 21 more at various planning stages.
 (b) Increased power generation capacity and cumulative sediment trapping with construction of the current dam portfo-
 lio (black squares indicate existing dams and white diamonds planned dams) and alternative portfolios with an optimal
 trade-off between sediment trapping and power production (grey circles). The arrow indicates a dam portfolio with
 higher power production, but lower sediment trapping, as compared to the current portfolio. (Optimal portfolios were
 identified based on analysis of 17,000 alternative dam portfolios (not shown). The optimal portfolio compares favorably
 to the currently planned development because of a different spatial configuration of dams in the network. (c) The current
 dam portfolio includes dams downstream in the Sre Pok and Se San rivers. (d) The alternative, optimal portfolio relies
 more on siting dams in the headwaters and in the lower sediment-yield portions of the 3S Basin. The optimal portfolio
 greatly reduces detrimental environmental impacts and reservoir sedimentation, and also produces higher economic
 benefits. Graph: Rafael J.P. Schmitt, adapted from Schmitt and Kondolf (2017)

34 Community-Based Conservation Initiatives in India:
       A Participative Movement driven by River Culture



Vazhayil, Alvin M.1, Wantzen, Karl M.1, 2

1
     CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, France
2
     UNESCO Chair River Culture, University of Tours, Tours, and CNRS UMR LIVE, University of
      Strasbourg, Strasbourg, France


"True democracy cannot be worked by twenty men sitting at the center. It has to be worked from below, by the
people of every village."
                                                                                                Mahatma Gandhi



                                                  Summary

This paper explores how River Culture (living with the river, learning from the river, identification
with the river) can be inspired by Community-Based Conservation Initiatives (CBCI) in river conser-
vation and vice versa. Humans are proactive in conserving things that are of value to them. When
humans see the ecosystem as a part of themselves beyond the utilitarian perspective, they develop
an emotional connection, which leads to taking sustainable actions for environmental protection.
The River Culture approach goes beyond ecologism, exploring the feelings and care for rivers that
people have, as we would do for a fellow human being. It brings various community actors together,
providing knowledge on the importance of living with the river. Such an idea that connects rivers
with our lives can motivate a society, eventually resulting in practical collaborative actions such as
community-based conservation. In the case studies discussed, environmental awareness through re-
ligion and education, volunteering mentality, quick reaction to a natural disaster such as floods, and
strong local governments incentivized people to take actions and transfer their ideas. CBCIs may
serve as examples of how to mobilize people to take action in favor of rivers or nature in general,
also in other places of the world.

34.3.1.2 Problems and drivers
The entire region has recently undergone a fast
increase of both, the population in the villages
and the intensity of land use. As a result, the riv-
er water is severely impacted by excessive pollu-
tion from agriculture and encroaching villages,
and water scarcity is caused by excessive water
withdrawal for irrigation (Kaur 2017). While
the agricultural impacts have not been quanti-
fied, the urban and industrial water pollution
of the Bein River is well documented. Most of
them come from the Hoshiarpur and Kapurthala
districts. The village Kheda Donaalon releases
300 m3 d-1 of untreated sewage, and the Bhulana
drain carries untreated effluents of 1,000 m3 d-1
into the river from Rawal and its colonies. In a
study conducted for the National Green Tribu-
nal, 33 out of 34 samples were not complying
with the sewerage discharge norm (CPCB 2019).
The most prevalent insufficiencies concern the
permanent filling up of the settlement basins and
the lack of connectivity to the sewage treatment
plants. As a result, large quantities of untreat-
ed wastewater enter the Beas and Satluj Rivers
(CPCB 2019, 2020). Toxic chemicals such as chro-
mium, nickel, zinc seep into the ground, pol-
luting underground water. The stagnation and
pollution of the waterbody provided a favorable
condition for the massive growth of water hya-
cinth (Eichhornia crassipes), a well-known aquatic
weed (Moza and Mishra 2007). The NGT tribu-             AMRITSAR
nal has held the Punjab government responsible          AMRITSAR

35 The River/Lake Chief System in China: A New Policy to Improve
        Environmental Quality in Hydrosystems



Cao, Yixin1, Wantzen, Karl M.1, 2

 CNRS UMR CITERES, University of Tours, Tours, France
1


 UNESCO Chair River Culture, University of Tours, Tours, and CNRS UMR LIVE, University of
2

  Strasbourg, Strasbourg, France



                                                          Summary

China is one of the fastest developing countries worldwide. As a negative side effect of econom-
ic growth, environmental concerns were often neglected in the past, resulting in severe pollution
and complicated governance structures to deal with environmental issues. This is especially true
for rivers and streams of China that have suffered for a long time from water pollution, hydro-mor-
phological and ecological changes, and mismanagement. In 2016, the government thus adopted an
innovative solution for river management: the national policy of River (and further Lake) Chief Sys-
tem. Closely following China's top-down administrative system, the River Chiefs are empowered
and well-placed to facilitate and enact wide-ranging collaborations amongst different governmental
departments. By strengthening the stewardship and accountability of River Chiefs, the system aims
at improving the efficiency and efficacy of many aspects of water management. The establishment
of the River Chief System is a paradigm shift in China's environmental management history, and the
short-term outcome is remarkable – water quality throughout the country has been improved and
quickly. However, many challenges still exist; the legality and the system's long-term sustainability
remain determined.

River Chiefs, taking the sustainable development
of the whole river basin as the goal. Simultaneous-
ly, as the river basin is a whole, the downstream
residents who have benefitted from the upstream
governance are obliged to compensate for the up-
stream river basin (Yang et al. 2004). Therefore,
the basin ecological compensation mechanism
should be established and promoted throughout
the country. The River Chief System can improve
the basinwide eco-compensation mechanism by
providing technical support, improving the mon-
itoring system through department linkages, and
diversifying and marketizing the compensation
model (Tang et al. 2019). In 2012, China launched
the first inter-provincial river basin ecological
compensation mechanism in the Xinan River

   We will hike to the source of a river and find
its beginning, whether it is a glacier on Mt. Rain-
ier giving birth to the Nisqually River in Wash-
ington or a small spring in West Virginia feeding
Deckers Creek. In Japan there is even a word
for this activity – sawanobori (stream climbing),
the act of following a river to its origin, often in
rugged mountain terrain where one must scale
ravine walls, swim through canyons, and ascend
waterfalls. Actually, the source is everywhere
because water evaporates, forms clouds, precip-
itates down on the earth below, and the hydro-
logic cycle continues its eternal journey.
   Studying maps of rivers, the meandering den-
dritic blue lines depicted on paper are so differ-
ent from the experiential reality of physically
being with the flowing water. Nothing compares
to being present with a river, incorporating all

   Originally, a natural creek, by the mid 1800s,
her backbone was straightened and dredged to
form a canal for commercial boat traffic. As with
so many other global waterways, the Gowanus
Canal began to be used not only as a transporta-
tion hub, but also as a convenient sewage dispos-
al system. By 1867, there were some enlightened
designs to install a lock system that would have
flushed toxins, but it was considered too expen-
sive, so one could say it was greed that brought
about this mess (gowanuscanal.org, qz.com, riv-
erkeeper.org).

   More than 20 coal plants dotted the shores
                                                           Creek, West Virginia
in the late 1800s, along with flour mills, tanner-
ies, chemical plants, and various other factories.
Slaughterhouses poured waste products, in-
cluding blood, directly into the water. The en-
gineers who had straightened this putrid body
had hoped the tides would flush out toxins, but
the waterway was open only at one end, and
wooden and concrete embankments did not al-
low for a thorough cleaning. Oxygen levels were
depleted. The canal became a breeding ground
for noxious pathogens. Raw sewage from new-
ly constructed buildings drained into the water,
as did storm runoff and pollutants. By 1910 you
could almost walk across this liquid sludge, due
to the accumulated solid waste! Decades passed

   In Asheville, North Carolina, the non-profit
organization, RiverLink (riverlink.org), works
tirelessly on behalf of the French Broad River to
promote conservation, recreational easements,
and greenway development. RiverLink members
and volunteers reclaim contaminated land, edu-
cate thousands of students each year, and ensure
permanent public access to the river throughout
the seasons. Students (grades 6–8) and faculty at
the French Broad River Academy have centered
their curriculum around the river. Imagine if ev-
ery school in the world chose to do this! Whether
the subject is social studies, humanities, or ge-       Fig. 36.25 Watershed meeting on behalf of the Portneuf
ography, the focus is on the watershed. What a          River in Pocatello, Idaho
great concept! This river provides inspiration for
art and writing classes, and a living laboratory
for scientific and mathematical explorations.
There are also lessons to be learned paddling
tandem in a canoe, which requires teamwork
and the ability to make quick decisions based on
surface conditions at any given moment.
   Again, and again, over many years, commis-
sions were formed, studies were done, plans
were made for ecosystem restoration on the
Gowanus Canal, Brooklyn, New York, but lit-
tle was accomplished. Conservancy groups, the

gently to protect the San Lorenzo River in Santa
Cruz, California and improve its water quality.
There is a history of pollution, and despite reg-
ulations and improvements, bacteria levels in
the water are sometimes so high the river vio-
lates the requirements for safe swimming. The
Water Quality Working Group including CWC,
the City and County of Santa Cruz, the Surfrider

formation campaign using social media, a blog,
youth education, mailers sent to households,
and radio public service announcements to ed-
ucate youth and adults on the responsibility of
everyone to help maintain this waterway. These
organizations have vastly improved river health
and the riparian environs by establishing the
Santa Cruz Riverwalk, with pedestrian and bike
paths on both sides of the river's course. Signage
has been placed beside the greenbelt walkways
with information about bird, aquatic, and river-
side plant life.

This book gives positive examples how humans and rivers have been,
and are still in some places, living in harmony. It analyses how this
knowledge can be transferred into modern river management schemes
and thereby it attempts to mitigate the deplorable trend of the decline of
biological and cultural heritages and diversities in and along rivers. A
harmonious way to live with the river includes i.a. respecting its natural
features and ecosystem services. This means that human land use forms
and cultures, including fishing, agriculture, navigation and river works
respect the natural hydrological patterns (Flood Pulse, Environmental
Flows). It also includes the physical-psychological-spiritual linkage of
the people to the river (e.g. worshipping, well-being, detention, and in-
spiration), and how these linkages serve as a motivation to take action in
favor of the river’s nature. Twenty-nine case studies from Africa, Asia,
the Americas and Europe, and 7 papers on overarching themes of sus-
tainable river management are presented.
Without claiming its completeness, we understand this book as a first
attempt to highlight the interactions between the biological-evolutive
populations of non-human biota and the biological-evolutive-cultural
populations of human beings, using the dynamic riverscape as the phys-
ical background.
The target audience of this book includes interdisciplinary scientists
from the fields of ecology, geosciences, social and political sciences, as
well as urban planners and managers of river ecosystems and riverine
heritage sites worldwide.
